articles.title_orig: Clemson scientist helps reveal a largely hidden world of giant viruses
articles.title_zh: Clemson scientist helps reveal a largely hidden world of giant viruses
articles.content_orig:
When we think of viruses, we often associate them with disease, but many viruses in nature have nothing to do with human illness.
A new study that included Clemson University microbiologist Barbara Campbell suggests that one poorly described group in particular — giant viruses — may be important participants in ecosystems ranging from ocean and freshwater systems to soil.
A collaborative international research team created the largest catalog yet of giant virus genomes. The collection includes 18,727 metagenome-assembled genomes, which are genetic reconstructions made from environmental samples from marine and freshwater systems, soil, rock, thermal springs, plant-associated environments and landfills.
After comparing the genomes, the researchers identified 8,508 species-level representatives, 712 previously unknown genera, 13 new viral families and a proposed new order called Mycodnavirales .
The study, published in the journal Nature Microbiology, provides new clues about the diversity and possible ecological roles of giant viruses.
“We’re interested in what’s going on out there in the environment at the microbial scale,” said Campbell, much of whose research involves the Chesapeake and Delaware bays .  Her group is especially interested in the ecological questions of “Who’s there? What are they doing? What and who are they interacting with?”
The study uses metagenomics to help answer those questions.
Most of the microbes in marine and estuarine environments are difficult to grow in the laboratory, and studying viruses depends on host cells. With metagenomics, scientists collect an environmental sample and sequence all the DNA in it. The genetic material comes from many organisms, and researchers use bioinformatic tools on high-performance computers such as Palmetto to assemble the fragments into larger sequences that can reveal the organisms’ identities.
“It allows us to look to see what’s in the environment without actually having to culture it,” Campbell said.
Despite their name, giant viruses can’t be seen by the human eye.
“They are giant, but giant is relative,” Campbell said. “You still need a microscope to see them.”
Bacteria are huge when compared to viruses. The smallest bacteria are about 0.4 microns in diameter, or one millionth of a meter. Viruses range in size from 0.02 to 0.25 microns. Most viruses are submicroscopic, meaning they are unable to be seen in an ordinary light microscope. They are typically studied with an electron microscope.
But some giant viruses are nearly the size of bacteria, and their genomes can exceed 2.5 million DNA base pairs. They may have hundreds of thousands of genes, including genes related to metabolism and protein production. That genetic complexity gives giant viruses the potential to influence the cells they infect in unusual ways.
Some giant viruses carry genes associated with producing proteins, a process other viruses leave to their hosts. Others contain genes connected to metabolism, stress responses and cell signaling.
“A lot of them have most everything needed to sustain life,” Campbell said.
That doesn’t mean they live independently. They still need host cells to reproduce. But their large genomes may allow them to manipulate host cells in more complicated ways than smaller viruses can.
According to the study, researchers found potential clues about the environmental roles of giant viruses, too. For instance, some groups contained genes associated with processing formaldehyde and breaking down aromatic compounds, including substances that can occur in industrial pollution.
The giant viruses in the study are generally host-specific and are not expected to infect humans. However, their impact could be felt by humans because they may help shape the health of oceans, bays, lakes and soil.
For Campbell, the results reinforce how much scientists still do not know about the smallest life forms in oceans and estuarine waters.
Viruses are part of what scientists call the microbial loop. Many giant viruses infect microscopic organisms such as phytoplankton and protists. When viruses break open their hosts, nutrients inside the cells are released back into the environment where they can be used by other organisms.
In low-nutrient marine and estuarine environments, that recycling can be especially important. Estuarine and marine phytoplankton are essentially single-celled plants that absorb carbon dioxide and produce roughly half the Earth’s oxygen she said.
“So knowing more about what makes them tick, and how they survive and die, is important, and studies like this give us an excellent starting point,” Campbell said.

articles.title_orig: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Starbucks enters Xinjiang in calculated geopolitical risk
articles.title_zh: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Starbucks enters Xinjiang in calculated geopolitical risk
articles.content_orig:
Hi, this is Anniek, writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses.
Starbucks struck one of Asia's most closely watched deals last year, selling a majority stake in its China business to a local private-equity firm. Now it is getting headaches at home over choices made by a partner that increasingly leans toward Beijing's priorities.
Starbucks Corp has taken its green apron to Xinjiang, a region where Western governments accuse Beijing of widespread human-rights abuses and where the U.S. restricts imports over forced-labor concerns.
The opening of two stores in Urumqi shows how the Chinese private-equity firm that now controls Starbucks' business in its second-largest market is willing to weather Washington's anger.
Starbucks completed the sale of a 60% controlling stake in its China operations to Boyu Capital in April. The venture aims to grow from roughly 8,000 stores to as many as 20,000, and Xinjiang appears to be a bold, if controversial, first stop.
The U.S. House Select Committee on China called the decision "shocking and morally bankrupt" for "a company that prides itself on social responsibility" and demanded the stores close. Its chairman, Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), was blunt in that statement headlined "Starbucks Serves Up Venti-Sized Genocide."
China's Foreign Ministry rejected the criticism, calling U.S. claims of genocide "a blatant lie" and saying Xinjiang has emerged as a region of "social stability, economic prosperity, ethnic unity and religious harmony." Beijing has long defended its security crackdown as necessary to counter terrorism and religious extremism, and denies allegations of "crimes against humanity" and ongoing repression.
Boyu — run by people who know China's politics well — wouldn't have missed the risk, said Ivy Yang, founder of Wavelet Strategy. "Boyu understands the sensitivity of Xinjiang as well as anyone," she said. In her view, the decision shows the firm weighed Washington's reaction and concluded that the domestic commercial opportunity mattered more.
The Hong Kong-based private-equity firm, co-founded by Alvin Jiang, a grandson of the late President Jiang Zemin, has long been seen as having close ties to China's political elite.
Starbucks has been losing ground on price and speed to local rivals, Yang said, and a new owner who's under pressure to deliver growth is likely to go where the stores aren't yet.
Molly Liu, chief executive of Starbucks China, in a recent statement , pledged to keep investing in the region.
Some, however, believe Starbucks' store openings cannot be read as a purely commercial decision.
"Chinese authorities have a strong interest in attracting prominent global brands to Xinjiang to demonstrate the region's stability," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group.
Beijing has spent years courting investment in Xinjiang. Supporting the region economically became a state goal after the controversy over Xinjiang cotton, said Yaling Jiang, founder of consumer consulting firm ApertureChina, and state television and social-media content have since turned it into a consumer aspiration.
But Xinjiang remains among China's poorer regions. Its full-year rural per capita disposable income only just topped 20,000 yuan ($2,983) for the first time last year, compared with 24,456 yuan for rural residents nationwide. The non-metropolitan median household income in the U.S. was $60,459 in 2023.
More than a dozen American brands have already ventured into Xinjiang, including Pizza Hut, KFC, McDonald's, Tesla and Burger King. But few have drawn comparable criticism from U.S. lawmakers.
And that expansion has gathered pace since 2023, according to GeoHey Brand Insights, a geospatial-data research firm, despite the landmark Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act signed into law in December 2021.
"Worsening geopolitics is inevitable, and must be priced into any exit negotiation," said Meng Shen, director of Chanson & Co., a Beijing-based boutique investment bank, of multinationals' interest in joint ventures with Chinese partners.
With U.S.-China ties steadying this year, Starbucks' Xinjiang stores are now a test of the climate for American business in China, Wang said — if Starbucks ultimately halts the project under U.S. pressure, it would send a negative signal to American businesses in China that commercial commitments can be overridden by political pressure from Washington.
That could make U.S. brands even more wary of Chinese partners and future deals harder to negotiate, she said.

Chinese manufacturers are eyeing the U.S. data center buildout as an opportunity, even as the two countries compete for AI dominance. "We can see very big potential in the U.S. market," said S.K. Lee, a global vice president at Singapore-registered Brightray, an AI infrastructure company. "The China market is equally important, but we can see that there's a stronger demand in the U.S."

articles.title_orig: Alleged unregistered agent of China set to appear in court
articles.title_zh: Alleged unregistered agent of China set to appear in court
articles.content_orig:
A suspected Chinese agent appeared in a Los Angeles federal court Monday after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's son near Seattle last year.
Orange County, California, realtor Wanying "Heather" Zhang, 34, appeared calm, dressed in a tailored, white zip-up jacket, sweatpants and white sneakers, with shackles on her wrists and ankles. CBS News was first to report that the FBI arrested Zhang on Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China.
In court, she spoke only to confirm her name and that she understood the charge against her of working as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government.
Zhang was represented by a public defender at the hearing.
Judge Steve Kim rescheduled her detention hearing to Wednesday to give Zhang more time to hire a private criminal defense attorney.
Zhang was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals until her Wednesday hearing.
The public defender, Chad Pennington, told the judge he believed Zhang intended to hire private counsel.
Her husband, Edric Ding, watched the proceedings, flanked by his sister, attorney Elaine Lori.
Standing at the podium, Zhang looked back at her husband briefly, but showed no emotion.
Lori and Ding declined to comment inside the courthouse and remained silent as they were questioned by reporters as they walked to their car after the hearing. When reached by phone on Sunday, Ding told CBS News, "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.
Three prosecutors represented the Justice Department: Scott Lara of the National Security Division's Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Amanda Elbogen and Colin Scott. They said they were not authorized to comment.
U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli posted a video on X of Zhang being frogmarched through the airport by federal law enforcement on Sunday, wearing the same outfit she wore in court on Monday.
A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of allegedly traveling to Seattle in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.
Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.
The FBI agent's affidavit claimed the government obtained text messages between Zhang and Chinese government officials evidencing the alleged surveillance.
In one exchange, Zhang allegedly texted her supposed Chinese government handler on the day of her alleged Seattle trip, "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," while footage from Ting-Yu's neighbor's security camera showed her "appearing to film" the president's son, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening, according to the affidavit.
As well as arresting Zhang on Sunday, FBI agents also searched her home in an upscale suburb of Irvine, California.
A resident of the neighborhood said she saw about 10 FBI agents searching Zhang's home on Sunday morning.
"Several of them were sitting at a table inside the garage," said the neighbor, who asked to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. "Even the ones standing guard were wearing gloves. They told us there was a search going on."
Zhang appears to have been renting the home, after selling her 6,030-square-foot, six-bed house a mile away for $6 million in June, according to property records.
A former neighbor told CBS News he was surprised that the young realtor couple could afford such an expensive property.
"She introduced herself as Heather," said the neighbor, who also asked to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. "She was super friendly.
"Usually, the people here, they're a little bit older, because the price of the homes is from $3 million to $10 million. But they were very young," the neighbor continued. "They did a lot of upgrades. Even though the house was almost brand new, they started changing so many things."
"Two years later, they only sold it for a little bit higher than what they purchased. It didn't make sense why would they want to lose money after spending all of that money," the neighbor added.
The Justice Department claims Zhang was working as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government from June 2025 to September 2025, and plotted her surveillance mission with Beijing officials during a trip to China in June 2025.
"The complaint in this case lays bare a brazen plot directed by the Chinese government to conduct a covert surveillance mission on U.S. soil targeting close relatives of a Taiwanese government official," Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division said in a statement released Monday.
"Wanying Zhang's arrest for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government makes clear how far China's authoritarian regime will go to advance its goals. However, this case also demonstrates the FBI's unwavering commitment to defending the sovereignty of our democratic allies and combating all attempts by the Chinese government - and any foreign adversary - to conduct transnational repression within our borders," Rozhavsky said.
The Chinese and Taiwanese governments have not responded to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court grapples with case on holding Big Oil liable for climate change
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court grapples with case on holding Big Oil liable for climate change
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court kicked off a new term Monday, with the justices wrestling with an attempt by oil companies to throw out lawsuits alleging they should pay damages for the impacts of climate change .
Although the case concerns a specific lawsuit the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, brought against Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy, the ultimate decision could have broad ramifications for more than two dozen similar lawsuits brought by cities and counties around the country.
The justices — lacking a ninth member because Justice Samuel Alito recused himself — asked tough questions of both sides as they tackled broad legal questions raised in the case. Alito’s absence raises the possibility of a 4-4 split ruling that would leave the legal issues unresolved while allowing the Boulder case to move forward.
Boulder officials say they face increasing costs because of the impacts of climate change, including efforts to minimize risks from wildfires. Just this summer, Colorado has experienced extreme heat, drought and multiple fires .
The lawsuit, bringing claims under state law, says Exxon and Suncor misled consumers about the impact that greenhouse gases produced by their products would have on the climate.
The companies deny the allegations and warn that if the Boulder lawsuit and others like it are able to move forward to trial, they and other energy companies could face crippling damages in the billions of dollars. They also argue climate change is such an inherently national and international issue that it cannot be the subject of litigation in state courts.
There was some sympathy from the bench toward the oil companies and the potential for substantial damages.
Chief Justice John Roberts, one of the court’s conservatives, wondered how many more cities and counties would launch similar lawsuits if the court allows the Boulder case to continue.
“Just to make sure I have a correct understanding. Presumably, if you prevail, the next day a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit,” he told Boulder’s lawyer, Kevin Russell.
Although Boulder’s claims are based on consumer deception, Roberts also seemed skeptical that the lawsuit was anything other than what he called “an effort to reduce emissions.”
On the other hand, Roberts, in an exchange with the oil companies’ lawyer, Kannon Shanmugam, said litigation brought in state court against out-of-state companies over an alleged harmful product is commonplace.
Other justices also seemed conflicted. Liberal Justice Elena Kagan at one point compared climate litigation with the wave of lawsuits against tobacco companies and drug manufacturers that sold opioids, which were allowed to proceed.
The oil companies have pushed back on such comparisons, saying that in the tobacco and opioid litigation there was a much more direct connection between the product and alleged harm to consumers.
But Kagan also wondered whether, as the oil companies argue, the Clean Air Act, which Congress passed to regulate air emissions nationwide, could foreclose the Boulder claims. A ruling saying state lawsuits are pre-empted by the federal law could be “the more natural and simpler route” of deciding the case if the court sides with the companies, she said.
A decision on those lines would be the narrower of two paths to victory for the oil companies, with Shanmugam pushing for a broader ruling that state lawsuits are prohibited under the Constitution.
Liberal Justice Sonia Sotomayor pointed out that even if the Clean Air Act bars states from seeking to cap emissions, the lawsuit does not seek to do that. “The Clean Air Act does not regulate marketing or advertising of fuel, correct?” she said.
The most vocal justice in backing the oil companies was conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who cited several court precedents that he said were “crystal clear” that air and water pollution are matters of federal law that the states cannot regulate.
“We don’t have to reinvent the wheel, because we’ve said this multiple times,” he added.
Overall, there appeared to be a lack of consensus on the bench about how to resolve the case, with one possibility that the court simply dismisses it, which would allow litigation to continue.
Lurking in the background are recent efforts by the Trump administration’s Environmental Protection Agency to eliminate greenhouse gas regulations under the Clean Air Act, an issue being litigated that could reach the justices in a later case.
“I think it is difficult to decide whether the Clean Air Act pre-empts these claims when we don’t know whether the Clean Air Act applies to greenhouse gas emissions when the EPA is saying it lacks the statutory authority to do that,” Russell told the justices.
The Boulder case was the first to be argued in the courtroom as the justices began a new nine-month term after a summer break. Other major cases already on the docket involve a challenge to bans on AR-15 semiautomatic rifles and two about the Trump administration’s hard-line immigration policies .
Alito announced last week he was stepping aside from hearing the Boulder lawsuit but did not say why. Liberal groups have said for months that he should recuse himself because he owns stocks in other oil companies that could benefit from a ruling in favor of Exxon and Suncor. Alito’s decision was a surprise, as the court had told NBC News in May there was no need for him to step aside.
The litigation is playing out amid a broader battle between oil companies and their allies on one side and groups advocating for action on climate change on the other.
State courts have become a focus, in part, because of a lack of action at the federal level, with the Trump administration rolling back Obama- and Biden-era policies seeking to reduce carbon emissions and speed up the transition to cleaner energy. The administration, which filed a brief backing Exxon and Suncor, has also sought to block renewable energy projects, with President Donald Trump calling climate change a “hoax.”
In a ruling in 2011 , the Supreme Court shut the door to making certain claims against energy companies over climate change in federal court, saying they were displaced by the Clean Air Act.
The proxy war over the issue has also focused attention on a chapter about climate science in a reference manual for federal judges. It was abruptly withdrawn this year after conservatives alleged the authors had a conflict of interest. Some also called for Kagan to recuse herself in Monday’s case because she wrote a foreword to the manual. She later said she did not even read the climate chapter.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.

President Donald Trump said Monday that the United States moved all of its long-range bombers out of the United Kingdom in response to "a threat."
Trump, when asked who made the threat, replied, "They would be linked to Iran ."
"Why would I leave them there?" Trump told reporters at the White House . "It costs very little money to move them."
The Associated Press on Sunday reported that the U.S. Air Force withdrew all of its B-1 bombers stationed at an air base in southern England, RAF Fairford, after a probe uncovered a planned terror attack. Those aircraft have been used in strikes on Iran.
The AP reported that the bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States.

articles.title_orig: Medvedev disqualified from China Open for hitting fan with a ball
articles.title_zh: Medvedev disqualified from China Open for hitting fan with a ball
articles.content_orig:
Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his semifinal against Novak Djokovic at the China Open after he hit a ball into the stands that struck a spectator in the front row on Monday.
The spectator was helped out of the arena, holding a hand over his left eye.
Djokovic was serving for the match at 7-5, 5-3 when Medvedev hit the ball into the stands in apparent frustration.
After a forehand volley winner from Djokovic, the ball bounced off the advertising boards and back towards Medvedev, who smacked a backhand that sailed into the stands.
The spectator who was hit was helped away as Medvedev stood on the court watching.
The chair umpire and tournament supervisor came down onto the court to talk to Medvedev, who didn’t appear to put up much of an argument with the disqualification. Medvedev then walked to the net and shook hands with Djokovic.
The incident was reminiscent of when Djokovic was kicked out of the 2020 US Open for accidentally hitting a line judge in the throat with a ball.
“A bit of a shock, to be honest,” Djokovic said. “I honestly didn’t see what happened. I hope that person is not badly injured. On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil, because I know exactly how he feels to be disqualified in a big match. … I am sure that Daniil didn’t want to do this intentionally. It just happens.”
Medvedev has a history of on-court behaviour issues. He was fined 6,000 euros ($7,000) for unsportsmanlike conduct after he smashed his racket seven times during a 6-0, 6-0 loss to Matteo Berrettini at the Monte Carlo Masters earlier this year.
Djokovic extended his perfect career record at the China Open to 33-0.
Aiming for a seventh China Open title in Tuesday’s final, Djokovic will face ninth-ranked Alex de Minaur, who advanced when Hubert Hurkacz retired due to an apparent injury midway through the second set of their semifinal.
It will be Djokovic’s second final of the year after losing to Carlos Alcaraz at the Australian Open.
With his ranking down to No. 11, this is the first time in eight years that Djokovic is playing a tournament without being in the top 10. It is also his first tournament since a first-round exit from the US Open. The 39-year-old Serb rallied to beat top-seeded Alexander Zverev in the quarterfinals on Sunday.
Against Medvedev, Djokovic was twice caught exceeding the time limit on the serve clock. After first receiving a warning, he was then stripped of his first serve on a crucial break point midway through the second set. But Djokovic still won the point.
Medvedev won only two of 18 break points as the pair of former No. 1s traded one gruelling rally after another.
The match was at the 2-hour, 29-minute mark when Medvedev was defaulted.
“I was three points away from the win,” Djokovic said. “It’s always a big battle with Daniil, and it’s so hard to play him when he’s feeling the ball well in slower conditions with a big serve. But we move on.”
De Minaur led 6-4, 3-2 when Hurkacz — who was barely able to run for balls in the second set — stopped playing.
The nature of Hurkacz’s injury was not immediately clear.
In the third round of the women’s tournament, which ends Sunday, six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek rallied past Donna Vekic 4-6, 7-6 (0), 6-2 and will next meet Iva Jovic, who beat Kamilla Rakhimova 6-1, 7-5.
Elina Svitolina beat Maria Sakkari 6-4, 7-5.
Later, Coco Gauff was playing 16-year-old Chinese wild card Sun Xinran, who recently won the US Open junior title.
US Open champion Elena Rybakina withdrew from the upcoming Wuhan Open due to a foot injury.
On Saturday, Rybakina lost her first match with the No. 1 ranking when she was ousted in Beijing by No. 118 Alina Charaeva of Armenia in the second round.
“I’ll take some time to rest and recover,” Rybakina was quoted as saying by Wuhan Open organisers.
Charaeva extended her breakout run by beating Sonay Kartal 6-4, 6-1 to reach the last 16.

Jinchao Wei and Ping Li are among 40 people facing denaturalisation actions in what the department described as the largest batch of such filings under the Trump administration. The civil proceedings remain pending, with no determination of liability, the DOJ said.

articles.title_orig: 2 People, Including Winter Haven High School Student, Killed in Florida Bus Crash
articles.title_zh: 2 People, Including Winter Haven High School Student, Killed in Florida Bus Crash
articles.content_orig:
Two people were killed after a major school bus crash in Winter Haven on Monday morning, according to the Polk County Sheriff's Office.
Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said the incident happened around 6:15 a.m.
He said the school bus was traveling eastbound on Lucerne Park Road when a westbound white Chevy Malibu crashed into it.
Judd said the impact caused the bus to lose control and tear off a tire. The bus then collided head-on with a Jeep and ultimately overturned.
As a result, two people were killed, including a 10th-grade student.
In addition to the school bus, three other vehicles were involved in the crash.
The school bus was carrying 39 people, including 37 high school students, who were on their way to Winter Haven High School.
The other two people on the bus were identified as the school bus driver and the driver's 9-year-old daughter.
The Winter Haven Police Department said Lucerne Park Road was shut down in both directions at US-27. It has since reopened.
The Winter Haven Hospital confirmed it received 22 patients, including 19 pediatric patients and 3 adults.
The hospital said it has treated and released all patients except one pediatric patient who was transferred to another hospital.

articles.title_orig: Woman accused of spying on Taiwanese president’s son arrested at LAX
articles.title_zh: Woman accused of spying on Taiwanese president’s son arrested at LAX
articles.content_orig:
The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News.
Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.
It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.
A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.
Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.
"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.
Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades . It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.
CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.
The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.
Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening.
CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.
Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.
The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.
"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.
The complaint claims  Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.
Holt's affidavit claims  Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.
She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.
On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.
Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.
Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.
Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA , Taiwan's national news agency.
Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.
Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang , 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.
Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.
The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.
New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.
In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.

"Permanent daylight saving time (DST) would expand access to golf at a time when the game is more popular than ever," Rolapp wrote in correspondence dated Oct. 1. That window is already tight, but when the clocks fall back, it closes entirely. An extra hour of evening light sounds simple, but for everyday Americans, it can be the difference between getting on the course and not."

Electric utility company Entergy Texas has appointed a new president and CEO to head the company’s broader customer-centric strategies following the departure of former CEO Eliecer Viamontes.
On Monday, Entergy Texas announced that David Borde will now lead the company. The move comes as Viamontes departed for other opportunities, according to a company release.
Headshot of new president and CEO David Borde. | Credit: Entergy Texas
Prior to accepting the role as president and CEO, Borde, who joined Entergy in 2009, served as the company’s vice president of utility strategy and regulatory initiatives. In that role, he supported Entergy’s objectives by leading regulatory and tariff filing efforts while  providing ongoing strategic and regulatory counsel.
During his tenure, Borde held several other key leadership roles, including serving as director of corporate development based in Texas, vice president of investor relations and within the utility finance business partner organization.
The company noted that this regulatory focus has allowed the organization to keep pace with evolving customer needs.
“David has extensive experience in utility strategy, regulatory affairs and utility finance, along with his deep understanding of our business and customers,” said Drew Marsh, chair and CEO of Entergy. “He is a thoughtful and proven leader, and he will build on the strong foundation in Texas while advancing our commitment to providing safe, reliable and affordable energy to the communities we serve.”
Before joining Entergy, Borde worked in the investment banking division of Citigroup USA and as a lawyer at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett. He earned a Juris Doctor degree from Duke University’s School of Law in 2001 and holds a business degree from the University of Paris.

articles.title_orig: California’s economy continues to dominate — topping $4.5 T in economic output, and remains the world’s fourth largest economy
articles.title_zh: California’s economy continues to dominate — topping $4.5 T in economic output, and remains the world’s fourth largest economy
articles.content_orig:
What you need to know: New federal data shows California has surpassed $4.5 trillion in economic production, dominates across sectors, and is a leader in increasing wages and salaries.
SACRAMENTO — While Fox News pundits and politicians in Texas and Florida attack the tentpole of the U.S. economy, Governor Gavin Newsom today announced that California has reached a new milestone as the first U.S. state to surpass $4.5 trillion in economic output. Since 2019, California’s economy has increased by over half, at $1.58 trillion. Recent data also shows that California’s private sector alone has now crossed the $4 trillion mark for the first time.
California didn’t become a $4.5 trillion economy by accident. It happened because working people show up every day and build, grow, manufacture, invent, and move to power this state. Small businesses take the risks. Workers put in the hours. Entrepreneurs bet on the future. That’s the California story, and nobody does it at our scale.
Newly released data from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis shows that California ranks first in economic output across almost every sector in 2025, including agriculture, manufacturing, technology, entertainment, healthcare, and wholesale trade. California’s economy grew by nearly $300 billion in the past year alone — the largest dollar gain of any state and $76 billion more than second-place taker-state Texas . These gains go deeper than just the GDP — on the individual level, total wages and salaries grew by 5.2%, and California is #1 for personal-income dollar gains this quarter. California also grew faster than Texas, Florida, and New York in 2025, expanding 3.5% after inflation.
California, the nation’s leader in manufacturing , also accounted for over 40% of total U.S. computer and electronics manufacturing and more than half of U.S. film and sound-recording output in 2025. The Golden State, home to 1.2 million manufacturing workers, pays more than $25,000 above the average non-farm wage, supporting families across the state.
The manufacturing jobs multiplier estimates that each manufacturing job supports three more in neighboring communities.
California manufacturers produced $391 billion in economic output in 2025, accounting for 9% of the state’s total GDP.
The state’s manufacturers exported $159 billion in goods in 2024.
Since 2021, California has invested over $215 million in over 675 contracts with employers to train over 194,000 workers in the manufacturing sector.
The Golden State represents only 11.5% of the U.S. population but is responsible for nearly 14% of U.S. GDP, 44% larger than taker-state Texas. California continues to lead the nation economically, outpacing all states and every developed nation , according to a Bloomberg analysis.
The state has more businesses than any other state, including Florida and Texas, supporting strong job creation and expanded economic opportunity for workers across the state. California is also home to more than 4.3 million small businesses , representing 99.8 percent of all businesses in the state and employing 7.6 million people .
As the world’s fourth-largest economy, California continues to lead the nation where it matters most — creating new businesses, attracting venture capital, driving technological innovation, expanding advanced manufacturing, growing high-tech industries, and producing more than any other state. In fact, the Golden State continues to be the #1 state for:

articles.title_orig: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.title_zh: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.content_orig:
Sixty-nine years ago this day, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first satellite to orbit Earth, opening the Space Age and setting off a race with the United States.
Ten years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty came into force.
In 1999, the United Nations started observing World Space Week – from October 4 to 10 – to celebrate the contribution of space technology for the benefit of humanity. Schools, space agencies, museums and astronomy clubs around the world hold stargazing nights, science classes, exhibitions and talks by astronauts and scientists.
Today, more than 80 countries have put satellites into orbit, and people from over 50 of those have travelled to space.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at which countries have done so, how many space travellers have been women, and what comes next for human spaceflight.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet astronaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
On board the Vostok 1 spacecraft, he completed one orbit of Earth at about 27,400km/h (17,025mph) during a 108-minute flight. He later ejected from the spacecraft and landed by parachute.
The mission demonstrated that humans could survive launch, weightlessness and re-entry, giving the Soviet Union a major early victory in the Cold War Space Race.
Six years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty entered into force. Signed by the US, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, it established that space should be explored and used peacefully and that no country could claim it as territory.
Less than two years later, NASA’s Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the moon. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on its surface.
There is no single agreed boundary for where space begins: most international bodies use the Karman line, 100km (62 miles) above Earth, while the US military, NASA and the Federal Aviation Administration count anyone who flies above 80km (50 miles).
Either way, it is closer than it sounds: if Earth were the size of an apple, space would begin about as far from the surface as the thickness of its skin.
By the Karman line measure, at least 746 people from 52 countries have travelled to space, including professional astronauts and paying tourists.
Some hold dual nationality, and some flew for countries that no longer exist, such as the Soviet Union.
The graphic below breaks down space travellers by country.
Two countries still dominate the list. The US has sent 369 people to space, and the Soviet Union and Russia have sent 138 combined. China, the third country to launch people on its own rockets, has sent 29.
Space remains a male-dominated frontier. Science fiction may be full of women commanding starships, but of the 746 people who have travelled to space, only 112, or 15 percent, have been women, about one in seven.
Soviet astronaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman to travel to space in June 1963. The US did not follow for another 20 years, until Sally Ride flew in June 1983.
The share of women is rising, though, largely because of commercial flights. More than half of the women who have flown since 2020 went up as paying passengers or guests on Blue Origin’s suborbital rocket.
Most people who have flown to space were in their 30s or 40s on their first flight, which together account for 85 percent. The median age is 40. Commercial flights have widened that range.
The youngest traveller, Oliver Daemen, was 18 when he flew in 2021. The oldest, Ed Dwight, was 90 years and eight months old when he flew in 2024, about two months older than William Shatner had been on his flight three years earlier.
In April 2026, the Artemis II crew flew around the moon and reached about 406,771km (252,756 miles) from Earth, breaking the distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970.
Next is Artemis III in 2027, a rehearsal in Earth orbit to test docking with lunar landers built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. NASA is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which aims to land astronauts near the moon’s south pole, the first crewed landing since 1972.
India plans its first crewed Gaganyaan flight in 2027, making it the fourth country to launch people on its own rocket. China aims to land astronauts on the moon around 2030.

articles.title_orig: Students vandalize Cornell building over handling of gang-rape allegations
articles.title_zh: Students vandalize Cornell building over handling of gang-rape allegations
articles.content_orig:
Hall housing Michael Kotlikoff’s office spray painted as demonstrators demand resignation of college president
Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
Mass protests erupted at Cornell University on Monday, with students criticizing officials’ handling of gang-rape allegations , demanding the president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administration building.
Thousands of students and faculty gathered for a demonstration, sparked by the high-profile case of a former student known as Jane Doe, who said in a recent lawsuit that she was plied with drugs and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. The case has prompted international outrage and intense scrutiny of college fraternities and sexual violence on US campuses.
Protesters shouted , “Ban the frats” and held signs saying, “At Cornell, rapists are safer than women” and “Stop rape culture.” Some demonstrators directed their anger at Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, arguing he had failed to keep students safe and chanting , “Kotlikoff, resign!”
The demonstration took place after some students had smashed a glass door at the entrance of Day Hall, a building that houses the president’s office, and painted messages on the facade at approximately 3am on Monday, the Cornell Daily Sun reported .
The messages in red paint read “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” and “AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED PROTESTORS ARE EXPELLED”. The security camera above one of the messages was also painted over.
The students who graffitied the building said in a statement to the student newspaper that they were protesting “the global systems of power that allowed this to happen in the first place”.
“We wanted to ensure that Day Hall, the center of Cornell’s administrative function, was not able to continue business as usual,” the statement added. The students’ painted message was a reference to arguments that campus officials had treated pro-Palestine protesters more harshly than students accused of sexual misconduct, with four student demonstrators suspended in 2024, according to the Cornell Daily Sun.
Kyle Kimball, a Cornell spokesperson, condemned vandalism in a statement on Monday.
“We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community. Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer,” Kimball said. “We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with University policy and applicable law.”
The student activists defended their actions in a manifesto obtained by the student publication. “We reject the dogma that would condemn our actions this morning as violent while excusing rape,” they wrote. “Property damage is not violent; condoning rape is.”
The demonstrations escalated as Cornell faces widespread backlash for its handling of Jane Doe’s case, with critics saying the university had been too lenient with the accused men and had failed the victim.
According to lawyers for Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. Jane Doe dropped out of Cornell after the incident.
A third fraternity member, who had already graduated, was barred from the Cornell campus, the New York Times reported on Saturday. Two more were reportedly given suspensions and disciplinary probation.
Two other men, the outlet said, were ordered not to contact the sophomore and required to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and to write “reflection papers”.
The lawsuit claimed that the seven fraternity members allegedly involved in the incident were “afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell”.
The university has said that claim does not accurately reflect what occurred. The accused men have denied all wrongdoing.
One student protester who addressed the crowd on Monday said : “Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support. How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?”
And a professor, according to the AP, said to applause: “Rape should not be inevitable.”
Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, who is also under fire for his office’s handling of the original allegations, announced last week he was reopening the case. Van Houten said Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago. Jane Doe’s attorney has pushed back on those claims and accused the DA of failing to do a thorough investigation after the incident.
Kathy Hochul , the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James , the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang rape at Cornell University.
Kotlikoff, the university president under fire, addressed the case in a video message on Saturday, saying the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, Kotlikoff said.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Lewis County: All 11 measles cases are in one town
articles.title_zh: Lewis County: All 11 measles cases are in one town
articles.content_orig:
LOWVILLE, New York (WWNY) - All 11 confirmed measles cases in Lewis County are in one town, according to the county’s public health department.
“All of the cases that we know about are in the town of Lowville right now,” said Ashley Waite, Lewis County public health director.
Waite said there are both children and adults affected, some of whom are related to each other. All are unvaccinated, and none of the children attend public schools.
On Monday, Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency over the growing number of measles cases across rural areas of New York.
Waite said the declaration will help slow the spread, as it will help health officials identify cases faster and provide more vaccines.
“When the governor declares a state of emergency, it’s opening up more resources for both the state health departments and the local health departments,” Waite said.
According to state data, there are no confirmed cases in Jefferson or St. Lawrence counties.
Health officials say the best way to prevent getting measles is to be vaccinated, which is 97% effective.
The CDC recommends everyone get two doses of the measles vaccine, first as a baby, and a second dose around the age of 4. Waite said if a child or adult is older than 4 and still needs the vaccine, it will still be effective to get it now.
“If somebody knows they’re not vaccinated, or wondering if they’re not vaccinated, they can reach out to their primary care provider. They can also reach out to us here at Lewis County Public Health and we can try to track down their immunization records, or we can offer the vaccine for them,” Waite said.
She said as long as someone is vaccinated, they should not worry.
“There’s little risk to the general public. The majority of our population is vaccinated,” Waite said.

articles.title_orig: Teenager loses hand in blast amid French school protest clashes
articles.title_zh: Teenager loses hand in blast amid French school protest clashes
articles.content_orig:
A teenager has lost a hand in a grenade explosion as the return of school protests in France sparked clashes with police.
The 15-year-old was seriously injured in the northern city of Lens on Monday. Unverified police reports said that he had picked up a stun grenade.
France had said it would close up to 500 schools as demonstrations over understaffed and rundown schools entered a third week. Critics have called for the authorities to temper their response to the protests amid claims of disproportionate police force being used against minors.
The youth, injured near the Auguste-Behal vocational high school, was taken to hospital in Lille. His life is not in danger, according to Pas-de-Calais prefect Francois-Xavier Lauch.
A police union source reported that the student appeared to have picked up a rubber sting-ball or ”de-encirclement” grenade, fired by riot police, in an attempt to throw it back before it exploded in his hand, the AFP news agency reported.
Public prosecutors said investigators have yet to establish whether the teenager picked up the device or whether it landed on him.
They have referred the case to police internal affairs, which is now engaged in six investigations into serious injuries that have occurred during the student protests.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray described the teenager’s injury as “humanly dramatic” but said he would not comment further until the circumstances were established. He said 190 students had been injured since the protests began.
The Lens incident has added to scrutiny of police tactics during the demonstrations. Amnesty International France has criticised what it described as disproportionate police force against minors, saying it was alarmed by reports of students being hit with batons and subjected to tear gas and rubber-bullet fire known as LBDs.
The rights group said many of those taking part were minors under 18 and called on authorities to ensure policing methods were proportionate and compatible with France’s human rights obligations.
Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon told CNews television on Monday that the priority was to “restore order”.
The Education Ministry said 589 schools had been disrupted on Monday, down from 735 on Friday, according to figures reported by Le Monde. Earlier estimates had suggested between 400 and 500 of France’s 3,700 high schools could be fully or partially closed.
Nationwide demonstrations erupted at the end of last month at a high school in a Parisian suburb over teacher shortages, before spreading nationwide.
Geffray said on Sunday that 24 schools had been burned or ransacked during the protests, with 78 teaching staff injured.
Reporting from a high school in Paris, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said students had set up a barricade in front of the building’s entrance using dustbins and fences.
“We’ve been talking to many of the students who have come out here, and what they say is that they are here to have their demands heard by the government. They say they are fed up with teacher shortages and often don’t have teachers for subjects like maths and English,” she said.
“They also tell us that they’re here to demonstrate to show solidarity with other high school students who are in perhaps poorer areas in France with less adequate facilities or in France’s overseas territories. They say all young people should have an equal right to education,” Butler added.
Unrest and confrontations were reported in several cities on Monday. News channel BFMTV showed images of police and students clashing in Lille, tear gas being used in Toulouse in the southwest, and a fire being set alight as people tried to break into a school in central Paris.
Carole Zerbib, head of the vandalised Lycee Vauquelin in Paris’s 13th district, said a “very determined” group wearing hoods and masks attacked her school.
While police and firefighters quickly put out the fire and the school was evacuated, suspending classes, Zerbib said it was “very violent and happened very quickly”, adding that the attack lasted 15-20 minutes.
Since September 28, about 5,000 people, mostly teenagers, have been arrested across the country and dozens have been injured.
Teachers and members of the public have also been attacked, while property damage costs are estimated in the tens of millions of euros.
Student unions have called for national demonstrations on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the largest in decades in the US
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the largest in decades in the US
articles.content_orig:
Neighboring states are also reporting hundreds of cases, with over 3,800 recorded across the country
Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials calculate, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades. The benchmark comes as neighboring New York declared a state of emergency about measles rates there.
Pennsylvania’s health department said Monday 1,004 cases of measles had been confirmed. Five Pennsylvania residents ⁠have died ⁠after ​contracting the disease, with 198 hospitalizations.
Lancaster county, with sizeable Amish and Mennonite populations, remains the hardest hit, with 391 cases, according to official figures. Cases numbers have risen over the past three months, with the highest number of infections in the 24-49 age range.
The numbers, however, are not included in a CDC count due to an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr over how to classify measles-related mortality.
Shapiro has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and Kennedy has publicly questioned whether the state’s recorded fatalities were directly caused by measles. The CDC – which Kennedy oversees – currently lists two measles deaths in the US this year.
Shapiro has expanded access to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in affected communities.
“I want every Pennsylvanian to know this: measles does not care about your county, your faith, or your social circle,” he said in August. “I urge everyone to take this seriously and to discuss any concerns with their trusted health care provider.”
In New York state, governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency on Monday as well, citing 108 cases in the state as of 3 October.
Ohio, which also shares a border with Pennsylvania, has also reported advancing numbers of cases, with more than 200 this year. Like in Pennsylvania, Ohio has a significant Amish population.
The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991. As of 1 October, the CDC reported 3,887 confirmed cases this year, along with the highest number of measles-associated deaths in decades.
In addition to Pennsylvania, outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest outbreak with 997 cases reported.
Health officials in Pennsylvania have said the state’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia and attributed the outbreak to low vaccination rates.
According to the Associated Press, the most recent outbreak to surpass 1,000 cases occurred in New York City in the early 1990s . That outbreak infected more than 4,500 people. During the 1989 and 1991 resurgences, 55,000 infections and 123 deaths ⁠were recorded, according to Reuters.
The domestic US spread of measles was eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status .

articles.title_zh: Brazil markets' Bolsonaro rally sends stock exchange to record high
articles.content_orig:
Brazilians will decide in just under three weeks whether to reelect incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva or oust him in favor of Flávio Bolsonaro — the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro — as both advanced to a runoff after receiving the most votes in the first-round vote on Sunday.
But the results of the first round are recalibrating how investors are pricing what the final decision will be.
Speculators on prediction market platform Kalshi now give Bolsonaro a more than 80% chance of winning the presidency. Before Sunday's first-round results came in, he had about a 60% chance to win. On Polymarket , Bolsonaro's odds are now 85%, jumping from 63% before the first-round count.
While Bolsonaro was seen as a narrow favorite to win the presidency before Sunday's first round, he was widely expected to trail the incumbent Lula in that initial tally, according to polls before the Sunday vote . This was the case even as Bolsonaro was favored to win a runoff. However, Bolsonaro secured more than 47% of the votes, beating Lula's first-round total by nearly 2 percentage points.
If no candidate receives a majority of the votes in the first round of a Brazilian presidential election, the two who get the most votes advance to a runoff.
Brazilian assets were on the rise following the result.
The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) was up more than 12% on Monday. U.S.-listed shares of Itau Unibanco gained 15%, and shares of Banco Bradesco surged 19%. Brazil's local Bovespa index was up 8%.
Investors broadly saw Bolsonaro as more favorable to markets , as the candidate is promising greater fiscal discipline. In June, Brazil's deficit-to-GDP ratio was almost 10%.
Lula is running for a fourth term as president. He won back the presidency in 2022 — after a 12-year stint out of the office — when he defeated then-incumbent Jair Bolsonaro. Lula's campaign has tried to tie Flávio Bolsonaro to his father's efforts to contest his 2022 loss and brand the son as corrupt .
The runoff in Brazil will take place on Oct. 25.

articles.title_orig: What impact will climate change have on malaria?
articles.title_zh: What impact will climate change have on malaria?
articles.content_orig:
Climate change could make a number of infectious diseases worse. I expected malaria would be one of them.
That’s concerning, given the huge global burden that it already carries: it kills almost half a million children every year.
But a more complex story emerges from the scientific literature. One where rising temperatures could actually reduce the burden of malaria in some areas, while making it worse in others.
What impact has climate change already had on malaria? Will it make the global fight against it harder or easier in the future?
These are the questions that I want to answer here.
Before we look at how climate change could change the dynamics and distribution of malaria in the future, we need a quick primer on the global burden of the disease today.
This is important because climate change could cause a decline in malaria in some regions, while increasing the prevalence in others. The impact on the overall global burden of malaria will mostly depend on what happens in the worst-affected regions today.
Malaria is an infectious disease present across much of the tropics and subtropics. In the map below, you can see the band of new infections across South America, South and Southeast Asia, and Africa.
The difference between sub-Saharan Africa and other parts of the tropics, though, is huge. Infection rates in sub-Saharan Africa are around 100 times higher than in South America and 50 times higher than in South Asia.
The fact that severe malaria is mostly an African story today is even clearer when we look at where people die from it. More than 95% of the 600,000 people who die from malaria every year live in sub-Saharan Africa. You can see this regional breakdown below. 1
But this chart also makes clear that within sub-Saharan Africa, there are substantial differences in the burden.
Around half of global deaths occur in West Africa — countries like Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, and Liberia. The rest are split between the central and eastern parts of the continent. Southern Africa has extremely low rates of malaria.
This dominance in West Africa is not just about population (we might expect more deaths in denser areas). As you can see in this map of death rates , those living in West Africa are at a much higher risk of dying from malaria.
These are the important background facts to make sense of this article’s focus. Most deaths from malaria occur in sub-Saharan Africa. Within the continent, West Africa is hit the worst. And children are most at risk: tragically, around 70% of malaria deaths are among children. That’s almost half a million children dying of the disease every year.
To understand the link between malaria and climate change, we need to know the basics of the disease’s “perfect conditions”.
Several mosquito species in Africa carry and spread malaria. A dominant one is Anopheles gambiae . It carries and spreads the parasite Plasmodium falciparum , which is what infects humans.
Over many decades, scientists have studied the ideal conditions for these mosquitoes to thrive. The spread of malaria peaks in these species at around 25°C. 2 Transmission drops close to zero below 16°C and above 34°C.
That means the suitability of malaria forms a bell-shaped curve like the one below. It spreads best at 25°C; this suitability drops on either side of it, and eventually becomes negligible.
Temperature is not the only thing that matters. How established malaria already is in a given country or region does, too. As do rainfall patterns: female mosquitoes lay their eggs in standing water, and larvae need water to develop. So, rainfall creates favorable conditions for malaria to spread. There is a limit, though: heavy, persistent rain often washes larvae away, preventing them from developing. An area with moderate rainfall is therefore a good breeding ground for malaria to spread.
Humidity can also have an effect. Adult Anopheles dry out in low-humidity air, so they often live longer in wetter, more humid seasons (and when they live longer, they do a better job of spreading the parasite).
The world has already warmed by around 1.4°C since pre-industrial times. 3
What impact has this already had on the prevalence of malaria?
A recent paper by Colin Carlson and colleagues, published in Nature , estimated the impact of historical climate change on the burden of malaria so far, and projected how this might affect it in the future under different warming scenarios. 4 The paper focused on the burden on children in Africa — as we established earlier, this is the most affected demographic, both in terms of cases and deaths.
They estimate that over the last century — from 1901 to 2014 — climate change has led to a small increase in the prevalence of childhood malaria across sub-Saharan Africa. By “increase”, they mean that rates were slightly higher than they would have been compared to a hypothetical scenario without climate change . The prevalence of malaria has actually declined in recent decades, but for reasons unrelated to climate.
Across the region, this increase was estimated at roughly 1 case per 1,000 children aged 2 to 10. To put this into context, around 24% of children (or 240 in every 1,000) in this region were estimated to carry the malaria parasite at the end of the study period. So, the overall impact has been relatively small and is quite uncertain. 59% of the study’s simulations showed an increase in malaria prevalence, with uncertainty ranging from a reduction of 4 cases per 1,000 to an increase of 6 cases per 1,000.
The bigger impact has been in changing the prevalence of malaria across different parts of the continent. Hotter temperatures might not have led to a large increase, on average, but they have affected its distribution.
Climate change has probably led to a decline in malaria in West Africa, but an increase in the southern and eastern parts of the continent. The following map summarizes this change: you see blue in the West but red, marking an increase, in the East and South.
Remember that West Africa is where the burden of malaria has been, and still is, the highest. A decline there due to climate change has been almost entirely offset by an increase elsewhere on the continent, which is why the effect, on aggregate, is very small.
The chart below shows malaria prevalence in two scenarios: the realistic one the world has lived through, and an alternate reality without human-driven climate change. Malaria has declined in West Africa due to climate change, but has increased in the other three subregions.
To understand why climate change has made things better in West Africa, but worse elsewhere, let’s return to our bell-shaped curve of where malaria thrives.
The study by Carlson and colleagues found results very similar to previous studies on the optimal conditions for malaria-carrying mosquitoes: transmission peaks at around 25°C.
In 1901, the average temperature in West Africa was around 26°C — very close to, but just past, the ideal temperature. 5 Climate change has increased temperatures, pushing them away from the optimum and down the slope.
What has happened elsewhere? East and Central Africa started below the optimum, at around 22°C, and Southern Africa far below, at around 17°C. Higher temperatures in all of these regions have pushed them closer to the optimum. East and Central Africa now sit at around 24°C, and Southern Africa at around 18°C.
It’s this temperature effect that has driven these diverging patterns across sub-Saharan Africa. The authors of the study did not find a discernible signal of climate change in historical drought and flood trends.
What’s crucial is that, while climate change has, on net, probably increased the burden of malaria across sub-Saharan Africa, its impact has been small compared with the many interventions and investments made to control and alleviate malaria. Malaria cases and deaths have not increased, but fallen substantially over the longer term.

American Karl ⁠Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday for developing optogenetics, a technique that uses light to control individual nerve cells in the brain.
The Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute said Deisseroth, 54, Hegemann, 71, and Nagel, 73, had been selected for their “discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”.
“This method [optogenetics] makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain,” said Thomas Perlmann, secretary general of the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute.
Anna Wedell, a professor in genetics and a member of the Nobel Committee for ‌Physiology or Medicine, said a new era in neuroscience had opened but it was only the beginning.
