articles.title_orig: How to protect your attention in an always-on world
articles.title_zh: How to protect your attention in an always-on world
articles.source: The University of Alabama at Birmingham
articles.content_orig:
Margaret Canter, Ph.D (left) and Maree Jones (right) There was a time when the internet was a briefly visited place. People logged on, did what they needed to do and logged off. That time is gone, and society’s attention now has completely shifted to the online world as digital technology has evolved.
As director of Social Media Strategy at the University of Alabama at Birmingham , Maree Jones has watched the shift happen in real time. Spending 16 years in a field that never stops, Jones has seen technology go from sitting on desks to riding in people’s pockets from the moment they wake up until they go to sleep. Drawing on her years of expertise in an always-online world, Jones provides insight on how to protect attention and focus in the workplace.
The challenge of protecting attention is a workplace concern, and it also is a critical component in mental health and emotional well-being.
Margaret Canter, Ph.D., clinical psychologist and professor of pediatrics in the UAB Marnix E. Heersink School of Medicine and Children’s of Alabama, speaks on the connection between attention and mental health, and shares her insight on attention protection and focus recovery. Canter’s work focuses on providing integrated behavioral healthcare to the pediatric clinic's patient population, which is children from birth through 18, and their families.
According to Canter, attention is a valuable resource because humans can give their attention to only one thing at a time, meaning what individuals choose to focus on and attend to must be worth it.
“When someone is able to focus and sustain their attention, they learn more and can be more efficient in completing their work or tasks,” Canter said. “If we are stressed or anxious about things getting accomplished, we may be preoccupied with those things’ getting done, which would negatively impact our attention.”
Difficulty paying attention and trouble focusing are symptoms of both anxiety and depression. If one already has difficulty paying attention, feelings of anxiety can become heightened, with mood and self-esteem being negatively impacted.
“In the age of social media, productivity isn’t just about how much work gets done. It’s also about how often we’re asked to stop what we’re doing and mentally shift to something else,” Jones said.
Likewise, if someone is already having feelings of anxiety and depression, individuals may not have the motivation to make the effort in their work, tasks and other responsibilities.
Jones says that part of what makes constant connectivity so draining is not the volume of work; it is the volume of decisions. With access to all kinds of information, the mind can be easily susceptible to burnout, and it can be hard to determine which information should be attended to. This persistent hum of pressure can be especially draining for people whose jobs depend on staying informed.
“Burnout has become an increasingly important conversation because we’re finally beginning to understand what long-term exposure to that pace feels like,” Jones said.
Smartphones allow access to all kinds of information at any time and place, including consuming the news via social media instead of traditionally. Because news segments are delivered in 30-second to three-minute intervals, sustaining attention for longer can be more difficult.
“When they’re wanting to read about a news topic or event, I encourage individuals to find one or two sources or individuals they trust and limit their exposure,” Canter said. “If we are intentional about our attention, we will not have the constant stream of information negatively affect our productivity and mood.”
In her role, Jones has the potential to be exposed to thousands of notifications a day. Each one, she says, carries a hidden cost of deciding on what and which information needs to be attended to.
For Jones, she has learned to recognize the warning signs that technology has taken the wheel. The antidote starts with treating attention as a resource worth guarding.
“By the end of the day, people who largely do digital work can feel exhausted because they’ve spent the day managing interruptions and making thousands of tiny decisions,” Jones said.
“Protecting my attention has become just as important to me as managing my calendar, because attention is what allows me to do meaningful work.”
For many people, including Jones, simply spending less time online is not an option. Being online is the job. So instead of avoidance, she recommends building boundaries around intention and learning to let technology work for her, instead of against her.
“I’ve adopted a mindset of being intentional with my time online rather than constantly immersed in it,” Jones said. “Sometimes that means giving yourself permission to mindlessly scroll but setting a timer. Sometimes it means unfollowing accounts that consistently leave you feeling anxious or discouraged.”
Some recommended ways to protect attention include the following:
When people are feeling stressed, they often seek distractions to take their minds off whatever is stressing them. While often associated with unproductivity, distractions can be a tool for attention protection and getting through a tough moment.
“Distraction is an excellent coping skill and one that I often use with children and teens in therapy,” Canter said. “Sometimes we need to get through a tough moment without doing something that would make the situation worse. However, it is important to remember that sometimes you need to come back to whatever is upsetting you and work through it, so it does not cause future problems.”
Having to respond to multiple people, whether digitally or in-person, can be taxing on the mind and attention. To balance responsiveness and attention, Canter encourages having windows of time when they are truly offline. This powerful strategy helps rebuild attention stamina and allows individuals to have higher-quality responses when coming back online.
“As a parent, I try to not have my phone with me during the time I’m helping my kids get ready for bed,” Canter said. “When I’m successful, I’m able to be more present for my kids, which feels good, and we are more efficient in completing the bedtime routine because I am not distracted by whatever it is I’m looking at or whoever I’m talking to on my phone.”
One of the biggest barriers to setting boundaries in terms of responsiveness, Jones says, is the fear of seeming unavailable.
“In workplace culture, we sometimes unintentionally equate responsiveness with value,” Jones said. “Responding quickly doesn’t always mean you’re doing your best work.”
According to Jones, the healthiest teams she has worked with communicate expectations and preferred boundaries clearly. Everyone understands what requires immediate attention and what can reasonably wait. That creates trust without requiring individuals to be constantly interrupted.
“For any communication methods, expectations should be discussed with your manager and your team,” Jones said. “Different jobs require different response times, and having those expectations clearly defined removes a lot of unnecessary stress.”
Digital fatigue is real, and much of it is fueled by the belief that instant communication should always be the norm.
“Just because technology makes instant communication possible doesn’t mean every conversation needs to happen instantly,” Jones said. “Digital work is cognitive work, and sometimes what feels like burnout may actually be decision fatigue.”
Away from work, Jones guards her attention just as carefully, keeping few apps on her phone and even fewer with permission to send notifications.
“Every notification is essentially asking, ‘Can I interrupt what you’re doing?’ Very few apps deserve that permission, especially in my free time,” Jones said. “Just because I work in social media doesn’t mean I have to live in social media.”

articles.title_orig: Lucid (LCID) Q3 deliveries drop 7% as it slashes production by 38%
articles.title_zh: Lucid (LCID) Q3 deliveries drop 7% as it slashes production by 38%
articles.content_orig:
Lucid (LCID) delivered 3,806 vehicles in the third quarter, down 7% from a year ago. It built only 2,954, a 38% cut from the previous quarter and its lowest production since early 2025.
The automaker says that’s on purpose. New CEO Silvio Napoli is selling down the unsold cars Lucid piled up in the first half of the year, and Q3 is the first quarter of 2026 in which it delivered more vehicles than it built.
Lucid released its Q3 numbers today , a month ahead of its earnings report on November 9.
Deliveries slipped 4% from the 3,953 vehicles Lucid handed over in Q2, and 7% from the 4,078 it delivered in Q3 2025. Production fell much harder, from 4,774 vehicles in Q2 to 2,954.
On paper, production is down 24% from a year ago. It’s worse than that. In Q3 2025, Lucid reported the 1,000-plus vehicles it shipped to Saudi Arabia for final assembly separately, and since the start of 2026 it counts everything that leaves its Arizona factory. Count both quarters the same way and production is down about 40%.
None of this is a surprise. Lucid eliminated the second shift at its Casa Grande plant in June when it laid off 18% of its staff, and it withdrew its target of building 25,000 to 27,000 vehicles this year. Nine months in, it has built 13,228 and delivered 10,852.
In the first half of 2026, Lucid built 3,228 more vehicles than it delivered. Most of that came in Q1, when a supplier problem with second-row seats held up Gravity deliveries for 29 days while the factory kept running.
In Q3, deliveries beat production by 852 vehicles. That’s about a quarter of the first-half pile.
Selling those cars is the biggest piece of Napoli’s “operating reset,” which targets $1.4 billion in cash flow improvements in 2026. Lucid expects $600 million to $800 million of that to come from inventory, about $500 million from lower capital spending, and roughly $200 million from operating costs. Its balance sheet showed $1.38 billion in inventory at the end of June, up from $1.11 billion six months earlier.
Lucid also said that demand for the Gravity “continued to regain momentum.” It didn’t put a number on it, and it doesn’t break out deliveries by model.
For comparison, Rivian delivered 19,248 vehicles in Q3 as the R2 ramped up. That’s five times Lucid’s total.
Lucid will exist until whichever Saudi Prince is bankrolling it decides to get another hobby.
I'm shocked it has lasted this long.
Cutting production is the right call. Lucid is losing about $1 billion a quarter, and building cars nobody has ordered only makes that worse. Napoli inherited the stockpile, and he’s dealing with it.
Based on the previously reported quarters, Lucid still has thousands of unsold cars to move and a Gravity that’s supposedly back in demand, and it still delivered fewer vehicles than a year ago. To be fair, Q3 2025 got a boost from US buyers rushing in before the federal tax credit expired. Rivian faced the same comparison and grew by more than 40% because it had a new product to sell.
And nothing is coming soon to change that. The Cosmos is delayed to the second half of 2027 , and the robotaxi deals with Uber and Bolt won’t move real volume for years. So Lucid has to get through at least another year on the Air and the Gravity at under 4,000 deliveries a quarter. The inventory selloff helps the cash position, but it only works for so long.

articles.title_orig: World Teachers' Day
articles.title_zh: World Teachers' Day
articles.content_orig:
World Teachers’ Day is held annually on 5 October to celebrate all teachers around the globe. It commemorates the anniversary of the adoption of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers , which sets benchmarks regarding the rights and responsibilities of teachers, and standards for their initial preparation and further education, recruitment, employment, and teaching and learning conditions. The Recommendation concerning the Status of Higher-Education Teaching Personnel was adopted in 1997 to complement the 1966 Recommendation by covering teaching personnel in higher education. World Teachers’ Day has been celebrated since 1994.
It is a day to celebrate how teachers are transforming education but also to reflect on the support they need to fully deploy their talent and vocation, and to rethink the way ahead for the profession globally.
World Teachers’ Day is co-convened in partnership with the International Labour Organization, UNICEF and Education International.
In 2026, the Day marks the 60th anniversary of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers. Six decades on, as the Recommendation is being revised, new challenges have emerged for the profession, from digital technologies and climate change to inclusion, migration and displacement. These pressures affect several dimensions of the status of teachers: their symbolic status, when teaching is not sufficiently recognized or valued; their professional status, shaped by limited autonomy, support or voice in policy-making; and their material status, compromised by salaries, workloads and working environments that do not allow teachers to fully exercise their role.
Under the theme " Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures ," the 2026 edition will centre on reviewing the current challenges related to teacher status and the strategies to address them, calling on society and policy-makers to protect, promote and elevate that status.
The global celebration organized at UNESCO Headquarters will feature high-level discussions on protecting and advancing the status of the teaching profession, as well as the award ceremony for the ninth edition of the UNESCO-Hamdan Prize for Teacher Development.
Other celebrations will take place around the world.
Joint Message from Mr Khaled El-Enany, Director-General of UNESCO, Mr Gilbert F. Houngbo, Director-General of the International Labour Organization, Ms Catherine Russell, Executive Director of UNICEF, Mr David Edwards, General Secretary of Education International, on the occasion of World Teachers’ Day 5 October 2026.
"On this World Teachers’ Day, UNESCO, the ILO, UNICEF and Education International call on governments and partners to stand with teachers by advancing the status of the profession  and  ensuring  that  every  teacher,  everywhere,  is  empowered  to  help  build more inclusive, peaceful and sustainable societies."

articles.title_orig: New UNESCO data: For every two teachers, the world needs one more
articles.title_zh: New UNESCO data: For every two teachers, the world needs one more
articles.content_orig:
A new fact sheet released by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics and the International Task Force on Teachers for Education 2030 examines the status of teachers, including how teachers are valued, supported and paid, 60 years after the adoption of the landmark 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers .
The fact sheet was released to mark World Teachers’ Day 2026 , bringing together ministers, teachers and education experts at UNESCO Headquarters in Paris to discuss how to strengthen the profession. Co-convened by UNESCO, the International Labour Organization, UNICEF and Education International, the celebration took place under the theme “Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures”.
Every learner deserves a teacher who is well prepared, well supported and empowered to thrive in the profession. Realizing this right depends on how societies value teachers and the teaching profession. In fact, the value we place on teachers reflects the value we place on future generation.
How teachers are seen by society shapes whether they stay in their jobs. In 75% of the countries taking part in the OECD's TALIS 2024 survey , fewer than 40% of teachers felt that their profession was valued. Those who felt valued were over 10% less likely to think about leaving within five years.
The stakes are high: 58% of the teachers the world needs by 2030 will be hired not to expand the workforce, but to replace those who leave the profession. The fact sheet shows where the losses are greatest: attrition rates are 7.2% in pre-primary education, 5.4% in secondary and 4.7% in primary.
The new data also reveals that pre-primary and primary teachers earn slightly less than other professionals with similar qualifications. Overall, in two out of five of the 68 countries analyzed, teacher salaries remain below those of similarly qualified professionals across all education levels.
Teaching also comes with a heavy workload.  Teachers spend an average of 19 hours in the classroom per week, but work around 60 hours in total, much of it includes unpaid preparation, marking and administrative tasks. In primary schools, the global pupil-trained teacher ratio stands at 28 to 1, the highest of any level.
The fact sheet offers practical recommendations for governments and partners. These include giving teachers a seat at the table when policy is made, setting professional standards and career paths, offering competitive salaries and targeted incentives for hard-to-staff schools, making schools safer and more supportive, and cutting back unnecessary workload.
UNESCO works with countries to increase the supply of qualified, motivated teachers by improving policies relating to them and supporting quality training which meets learners’ needs. Special focus is placed on Africa, inclusion, gender sensitivity and digital technologies.
UNESCO and the ILO have also launched a joint revision of the 1966 Recommendation , guided by an Independent Expert Group through mid-2027.
As the work moves forward, the evidence is clear: attractive, respected and supported teaching professions are the foundation of quality education for every learner.

articles.title_orig: Trump: U.S. willing to help Russia with potential pneumonic plague outbreak
articles.title_zh: Trump: U.S. willing to help Russia with potential pneumonic plague outbreak
articles.content_orig:
A 28-year-old lab researcher at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and dangerous pathogens died of pneumonia of an “unknown” origin.
The Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute operates in Siberia, where several other people are quarantined. Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that oversees infectious disease, has downplayed the link between the researcher’s death and her work, but the case has prompted questions about the type of plague that causes pneumonia.
The US State Department and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said they are monitoring the situation closely. The World Health Organization said Monday it’s in contact with Russian health authorities to verify what happened, what testing is underway and any potential international public health implications.
Dozens quarantined after researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies of ‘unknown’ infection
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” a WHO spokesperson said, adding that its risk assessment would be updated once more information was available.
Pneumonic plague is a rare, deadly lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Scientists consider pneumonic plague the most dangerous form of the infection.
There are other forms of plague stemming from Y. pestis that attack different parts of the body.
The most common form, bubonic plague, often develops after a flea bite or when the bacterium enters through a cut or break in the skin. The infection triggers swollen, painful lymph nodes and can progress to septicemic plague.
Septicemic plague infects the bloodstream, potentially leading to organ failure, it can also come directly from a flea bite.
Pharyngeal plague attacks the throat after someone eats infected meat.
Pneumonic plague is the only form of the bacterial infection that passes directly from person to person. Respiratory particles carry it when a person coughs or sneezes. Droplets from infected animals can also transmit it.
The last documented person-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague in the United States dates back to 1924, during an outbreak in Los Angeles .
With pneumonic plague, particles lodge in the lungs and can trigger severe pneumonia, making breathing difficult. Symptoms can begin within 24 hours of infection.
Other symptoms include fever, chills, headache, body aches, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Without treatment, it is nearly always deadly.
Doctors can treat plague with at least 10 to 14 days of antibiotics. Most commonly they use ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin, and streptomycin. Patients that get antibiotics within the first 24 hours of infection have the best chance of surviving.
Doctors may also support someone with supportive care and provide supplemental oxygen, fluids and encouragement to rest.
Although plague vaccines have been in use since the 19th century, it wasn’t clear they offer protection from pneumonic plague.
The WHO doesn’t recommend vaccination , except for high-risk groups such as laboratory personnel who are constantly exposed to the risk of contamination.
Although people may be most familiar with plague from reading the Bible or historical literature — or as a metaphor to describe broader pestilence and poverty, according to infectious disease expert Dr. Tyler Evans — it persists today.
Known as the “Black Death” in the 14th century, the infection killed more than 50 million people in Europe. While antibiotics have made it more manageable, it remains present on every continent except Oceania.
Since the 1990s, most human cases have occurred in Africa, according to the WHO.
The last US death from pneumonic plague occurred in Arizona in July 2025, according to the CDC . The young man worked with sick cats and is believed to have contracted the infection from the animals. No one else exposed to the cats reported getting sick.
Evans, who wrote “ Pandemics, Poverty and Politics: Decoding the Social and Political Drivers of Pandemics from Plague to Covid-19 ,” says the risk for plague is “getting worse as the result of ecological changes and particularly with the US pulling back on our public health infrastructure and measures.”
Plague, at least, can be quick to diagnose, he said. And “the antibiotics, first and second line, are very effective for this.”
WHO has said the risk to the general population appears to be low.
People with pneumonic plague feel sick very quickly, which can slow potential spread, according to Dr. Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.
“It’s very difficult for someone to even walk, do their daily activities, let alone travel,” Dalal said. People can develop symptoms as early as 24 hours after exposure.
There are no direct flights between Russia and the US, he said, so by the time an infected person would reach the US they would likely already be exhibiting symptoms.
“Of course, you have to be careful, and you should keep this at the back of your mind … The world is a little village now, as I say — connected to each other. But at this point in time, compared to what we have been seeing, like during the Covid pandemic, this is not of that magnitude as of now, and hopefully remains contained as it is.”
For people around patients with plague, WHO recommends avoiding direct contact with those who are sick and urges caution around infected body fluids.
Workers caring for patients with pneumonic plague must wear standard protective equipment and may also take preventive antibiotics.
In case of exposure, health officials will also monitor family members and other close contacts of an infected person and provide them with antibiotics before they become ill. They also recommend routine hand-washing with soap and water.

articles.title_orig: Statin Side Effects: What the Evidence Shows
articles.title_zh: Statin Side Effects: What the Evidence Shows
articles.content_orig:
The list of possible side effects attributed to statins is long: muscle pain, memory problems, depression , sleep disturbances, diabetes, and liver damage. However, a meta-analysis by the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists’ (CTT) Collaboration in The Lancet calls many of these associations into question. At the same time, the study confirmed that certain effects on muscles, the liver, and glucose metabolism can indeed occur. What matters, however, is their magnitude — and that is usually significantly lower than what the public criticism of these drugs would suggest.
The new meta-analysis includes 19 double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials involving 123,940 participants with a median follow-up period of 4.5 years. In addition, the authors evaluated four trials involving 30,724 participants in which more intensive statin therapy was compared with less intensive statin therapy.
They examined 66 adverse events listed in the package inserts for atorvastatin , fluvastatin , pravastatin , rosuvastatin , and simvastatin . Aside from the known effects on muscle function and glucose metabolism, only four of the 66 events remained statistically significant after adjusting for various confounding factors:
Elevated transaminase levels occurred at a rate of 0.30% per year with statins and 0.22% per year with placebo. The relative risk (RR) was 1.41. Other abnormal liver function test values were observed in 0.25% of cases per year with statins vs 0.20% of cases per year with placebo. Changes in urine composition were observed in 0.21% of cases per year with statins vs 0.18% of cases per year with placebo, and edema was observed in 1.38% of cases per year with statins vs 1.31% of cases per year with placebo.
For the remaining 62 endpoints, there was no significant evidence of harm after statistical adjustment for potential confounders.
Among the most common concerns expressed on social media is the fear of impaired memory and cognitive function. At first glance, this concern appears biologically plausible, given that cholesterol is essential for neuronal membranes and myelin. However, the brain’s cholesterol metabolism operates largely independently of peripheral low-density lipoprotein ( LDL ) metabolism.
Clinically, there is no convincing evidence of harm. The recent CTT analysis showed no robust association between statin therapy and cognitive impairment.
Another recent meta-analysis included 42 randomized trials involving 150,405 participants. For lipid-lowering therapies overall, the RR of neurocognitive events was 0.99 (95% CI, 0.88-1.12). For statins alone, the RR was 0.94 (95% CI, 0.72-1.25). No relevant negative effect was found in five specifically examined cognitive domains, namely attention, processing speed, executive function, working memory, and memory.
Depression and sleep disorders are also often attributed to statins. However, both conditions occur frequently in the age group of patients typically prescribed statins. What matters, therefore, is not whether they occur during therapy but whether they are more frequent than without statins.
The new CTT meta-analysis found no evidence to support this. Neither depression nor sleep disturbances were significantly more common among statin users than among those taking a placebo. In the case of depression, observational data even pointed in the opposite direction.
A meta-analysis from 2025 included 15 studies from 10 countries with 5,403,692 participants. Statin users had a lower risk for depression, with a pooled odds ratio of 0.84 (95% CI, 0.74-0.96). However, the heterogeneity of the data was considerable. Therefore, no antidepressant effect can be inferred from these predominantly observational studies. However, they do not suggest a significant depression-promoting effect.
The situation is more nuanced when it comes to muscle pain. There is indeed a causal effect here, but the absolute magnitude is small.
The CTT Collaboration analyzed individual-level data from 19 placebo-controlled trials involving 123,940 participants. During a median follow-up of 4.3 years, 16,835 of 62,028 patients on statins (27.1%) reported muscle pain or muscle weakness. In the placebo group, the figure was 16,446 out of 61,912 participants (26.6%). The RR was 1.03 (95% CI, 1.01-1.06).
The difference was primarily concentrated in the first year of treatment. During this period, statins increased the RR by 7% (RR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.04-1.10). In absolute terms, this corresponded to 11 additional muscle-related events per 1000 person-years. After the first year, no significant excess was detectable (RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.96-1.02).
The authors’ calculation is particularly illustrative: Of 15 muscle complaints reported by patients in the first year of statin therapy, statistically, only one was actually attributable to the medication. In the randomized trials, more than 90% of the muscle complaints reported by patients who were prescribed statins were therefore, mathematically speaking, not attributable to the statin.
The SAMSON study demonstrated just how difficult the question of causality can be. The study included 60 patients who had previously discontinued statins due to side effects. They underwent 12 1-month phases: four with 20 mg of atorvastatin, four with a placebo and four without any medication at all. A total of 49 patients completed the entire study program.
Participants rated the intensity of their symptoms daily via an app on this scale:
The mean symptom score was 8.0 points during the months without medication. It increased to 16.3 points during periods when participants were taking atorvastatin, but it rose nearly as much — to 15.4 points — during placebo treatment. There was no significant difference between atorvastatin and placebo ( P = .39). In other words, about 90% of the added symptom burden seen with atorvastatin, compared with that during the medication-free months, was also seen with placebo.
The larger StatinWISE study yielded similar results. Of 200 patients who had discontinued a statin due to muscle symptoms or intended to do so, 151 were included in the primary analysis. The difference in muscle symptom scores between atorvastatin and placebo was only -0.11 points on a 0-10 point scale (95% CI, -0.36 to 0.14; P = .40). Due to intolerable muscle symptoms, 9% discontinued treatment during the statin period and 7% discontinued treatment during the placebo period.
After the research team communicated the individual study results, 74 of 113 patients (65.5%) reported that they had already resumed statin therapy or intended to do so. After 15 months, 58 of 113 (51.3%) were indeed prescribed a statin again.
There is a biological explanation for why a small proportion of muscle symptoms are actually caused by statins. Statins inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase, thereby blocking the mevalonate pathway. This not only reduces cholesterol synthesis but also affects isoprenoid synthesis, protein prenylation, and coenzyme Q10 formation.
Discussions focus on changes in mitochondrial energy production, intracellular calcium homeostasis, and various signaling pathways in muscle cells. Mechanistic studies also point to possible effects on mitochondrial enzyme complexes and calcium ATPases.
However, the clinical data put these mechanisms into perspective: If 27.1% of patients on statins and 26.6% of patients on placebo report muscle symptoms, the impact on the mevalonate pathway cannot account for the majority of the observed complaints.
The same applies to coenzyme Q10. A decrease in its levels is biologically plausible. However, this does not mean that a Q10 deficiency is the most common cause of statin-associated muscle pain.
The evidence is clearer regarding glucose metabolism. Statins increase the risk for newly diagnosed diabetes, and the effect is dose dependent.

Quebec City — Technimount EMS (Technimount), a leading provider of mounting solutions for medical devices, is proud to announce that its Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL has been selected as a finalist for the 2026 EMS World Innovation Awards.
Designed specifically for critical care air transport, the Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL transforms a LifePort AeroSled TS stretcher, typically used for adult and pediatric patients, into a neonatal transport system within seconds. The platform securely mounts the Dräger Isolette TI500 incubator while allowing care teams to quickly return the stretcher to standard patient care when neonatal transport is no longer required. By eliminating the need to dedicate a stretcher exclusively to neonatal care, this solution helps air medical teams to optimize equipment utilization while increasing operational flexibility.
At the heart of the system is Technimount’s proprietary XClamp Technology, which remains installed directly onto the stretcher without interfering with its regular use. When neonatal transport is required, the platform can be rapidly installed without tools. A dual quick-release latch system, one securing the platform to the stretcher and the other anchoring the incubator, allows for fast installation and removal. Engineered with the space constraints of aircraft environments in mind, the compact platform remains within the dimensions of the AeroSled TS while providing a secure solution for neonatal transport. The system has been rigorously tested to meet applicable sections of FAA regulations 14 CFR §§ 23 and 25.
The Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL is also designed for seamless compatibility with Technimount’s Xtension Pro Assistant – LP, a previous EMS World Innovation Awards-winning solution. Together, the systems provide teams with the ability to securely manage the incubator and essential medical devices required for neonatal critical care throughout transport.
“Being selected as an EMS World Innovation Awards finalist for a tenth year is an important recognition of the work our team continues to put into solving real challenges faced by critical care transport professionals,” said Carl Bouchard, Founder and CEO of Technimount System. “The Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL was developed to give air medical teams greater flexibility without compromising safety or efficiency, and we are proud to see this innovation recognized by the EMS industry.” Concluded Mr. Bouchard
Technimount EMS is a leading provider of mounting systems designed to safely secure medical devices during transport. Technimount EMS addresses the safety needs of patients and staff during ground or air emergencies and Critical Care Transport, establishing itself as a standard in the Emergency Medical Services industry.

articles.title_orig: Will Powerful Countries Back the UN Chief the World Needs?
articles.title_zh: Will Powerful Countries Back the UN Chief the World Needs?
articles.content_orig:
As the United Nations continues its search for a new leader , Binaifer Nowrojee, president of the nonprofit Open Society Foundations, described the kind of secretary-general that the world wants. But is it the same person that the five permanent members of the Security Council — Britain, China, France, Russia and the US — want, PassBlue asked her.
“We need a secretary-general that is bold, that is not scared to speak truth to power,” Nowrojee told PassBlue on Sept. 24, during an interview that touched on many global issues, including the race to choose the UN’s next top diplomat.
The 15-member Security Council ultimately recommends a candidate to the General Assembly for approval this year, as planned. But the process is currently going through an informal straw-poll phase to assess its candidate of choice.
The latest poll was held by the Council on Sept. 29, after three in July, August and early September, respectively, and like the others before it, the P5, as they are known, have yet to publicly show their hands on who they want to lead the 81-year-old UN. Each P5 has a veto, which can block a substantive Council decision despite majority support and thus end a candidate’s aspirations. A nominee needs to have at least nine votes from the Council and no veto to win the coveted recommendation to the Assembly.
Aglaia Balta, Greece’s permanent representative to the UN and the Council’s monthly rotating president, said on Oct. 1 that members would be consulted on using color-coded ballots in the next two straw polls, slated for midmonth and end of the month. The color ballots distinguish the P5’s votes from those of the 10 elected members, revealing whether a candidate faces opposition from a permanent member without identifying which country cast the no vote.
The candidates, now numbering seven, after Michelle Bachelet of Chile dropped out on Sept. 20, have been straddling a tightrope in their respective campaigns, avoiding statements that could put them at crossroads with the P5. Despite the balancing act, some P5 have publicly signaled reservations about candidates. Bachelet, Chile’s two-time president, announced her withdrawal after poor results in the first three informal ballots.
Opposition from Washington was a hurdle she could not surmount because of her perceived pro-abortion stance and other matters. (Relevant US officials, for starters, never met with her, according to a diplomat familiar with her campaign.) China has said it would prefer a woman secretary-general. That could complicate the bids of candidates like Rafael Grossi of Argentina, Macky Sall of Senegal and Olara Otunnu of Uganda. Grossi also faces a potential block from Russia, which has reportedly suggested it may oppose candidates with European Union or NATO citizenship.
Besides being Argentine, Grossi holds Italian citizenship. Maria Fernanda Espinosa, a candidate who is a former vice president of Ecuador and is backed by Antigua and Barbuda, has Spanish citizenship. So far, Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett have led the informal polls, but neither has emerged as an obvious consensus choice for the Council to recommend to the General Assembly. Color-coded ballots will better reveal their chances.
The interview has been edited for clarity and condensed for brevity. Some questions have been reordered for better flow.
PassBlue: Given the UN’s financial crisis, political tensions and struggles to resolve conflicts and fund development work, would a woman secretary-general step onto a glass cliff?
Binaifer: The United Nations has carried us well for the last 80-plus years, and there’s been great steps forward on a variety of issues through the UN and a rules-based world order, and people still want that. Governments still want that, but we are now at a point where the world is different. When the UN was set up, it was four or five empires that actually set it up and have presided over it. So there are inequalities and privileges that were built in that no longer fit today’s world.
Today, we don’t have a world of four or five empires. We have a world of 193 countries that sit and want a place at the table. Demographics are different. Eighty-five percent of the world’s population is now sitting in the global majority, only 15 percent in Europe and the United States. The UN has reached the end of how it can function in the way it’s functioned, and a reset is required, and that is the case for any organization.
The most important thing we need right now is a secretary-general who is visionary and bold and is ready to take this organization into the future. As the first woman to lead the Open Society Foundations, it is incredible to me that over 80 years, not a single woman has served as the UN secretary-general.
It is symbolic of the types of exclusions that have limited the abilities of the UN, even as it has espoused equality, even as it espoused human rights principles; it’s an important thing that it walks the talk internally of what it needs to do. We need a secretary-general who will lead us into the future that this next generation is going to live in.
PassBlue: What does the world need from the next secretary-general that might conflict with the P5’s priorities?
Binaifer: We need a secretary-general that is not scared to speak truth to power, that substantively can identify the key issues we need to focus on in this next century and is not scared to make some of the hard decisions that will require. We also need a secretary-general that is a bridge builder. They still have to work with member states. They still have to build coalitions around the agendas. But let’s not have a secretary- general that relinquishes the entire reform agenda and limits it only to budgets and headcounts. We have a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to press a reset button. Let’s do it properly.
PassBlue: How do you see African countries engaging in multilateral, bilateral and trilateral AI discussions and using the technology?
Binaifer: First of all, we know Africa is the youngest continent, and every one of those young people has a phone in their hand, so we know that there’s a lot of familiarity and that young Africans are leaning into technology. They’ll lean into artificial intelligence. They may not be the architects of the structure, but they will be the users, and they will innovate and find ways to have this integrated into their lives.
What we want to ensure is that the harms that we are seeing in places where children or hate speech, those kinds of things, that African governments take steps to put in a regulatory environment, because now we know those lessons. We see Australia stopping social media for children under 16. We know that women politicians, for example, get much more hate and abuse online compared to male politicians. So African governments can actually make policy decisions to limit the harms but also benefit, to have their young people benefit from the good possibilities that that technology and artificial intelligence will bring.
PassBlue: How can African countries move beyond consuming technology to creating economic benefits for young people and for their national economies?
Binaifer: There’s huge innovation in Africa on many levels. Take a place like Kenya, where technology for money transfers with M-Pesa happened long before other countries were doing it, and you find very savvy tech people in Gen Z organizing protests on social media to call on the government to do things about their issues. We also see innovation in organizations like Gearbox in Kenya or others, and the difference between the US and Africa in terms of why does innovation actually appear in the US in the tech space. Because the US government has invested in providing funds for innovation.

articles.title_orig: Disease ecologist on the emergence of the new world screwworm and how to stop it
articles.title_zh: Disease ecologist on the emergence of the new world screwworm and how to stop it
articles.content_orig:
As a new parasite with flesh-eating larvae threatens the nation's livestock industry, a team of Virginia Tech researchers will be on the frontlines of defense.
Led by Luis Escobar, an associate professor of fish and wildlife conservation, the team is working on one of 40 breakthrough projects funded through the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to develop an integrated preparedness and response system against the re-emergence of the new world screwworm in the Americas.
“Preventing a screwworm invasion protects food production, food prices, rural economies, family farms, wildlife populations, companion animals such as dogs and horses, and public health because the screwworms can also affect people,” said Escobar.
Earlier this summer, the USDA confirmed that the new world screwworm fly reached south Texas, threatening the livestock industry for the first time in decades.
Screwworm-related losses exceeded $200 million annually in the 1950s, the equivalent of roughly $1.8 billion today, before eradication efforts succeeded.
According to Escobar, mitigation measures include mandatory physical inspections and anti-parasitic treatments for cattle at southern border ports, as well as stricter movement requirements for animals entering Texas.
As part of the project, Virginia Tech will expand collaborations with Texas A&M, North Carolina State University, the University of Kansas in the United States, Universidad de San Carlos, and Universidad del Valle in Guatemala.
“Rather than addressing one aspect of screwworm control, this project creates a complete decision-support framework that connects surveillance, genetics, producer behavior, and predictive modeling,” Escobar said.
Luis Escobar is an associate professor in the College of Natural Resources and Environment at Virginia Tech. He is a member of the Pandemic Prediction and Prevention Destination Area, the Invasive Species Collaborative, and the Fralin Life Sciences Institute’s Center for Zoonotic and Arthropod- borne Pathogens and Global Change Center.
His research focuses on biogeography, ecology, and evolution of infectious diseases across landscapes.

articles.title_orig: In a divided world, St. Francis points the way forward
articles.title_zh: In a divided world, St. Francis points the way forward
articles.content_orig:
Author: Br. Murray Bodo, OFM
Date Published: October 05, 2026
In declaring 2026 the year of St. Francis , Pope Leo has once again called attention to the depth and breadth of the world’s interest in St. Francis. In this, the 800th anniversary year of his death , Francis has emerged as a saint who is as relevant today as he was in his lifetime.
We live in a time of division and upheaval in the world, with wars cropping up in the Middle East and Eastern Europe, and with hateful rhetoric and divisive decisions that are separating people. The good among us are longing and praying for peace daily: peace in the world and peace of heart. We long for models and look to saints for guidance about how we are to live our lives. Again and again, we turn to Francis of Assisi as the Christian example of a peacemaker who found peace of heart and preached peace and good by embracing Jesus and His Gospel of Peace and Love. “May the Lord give you peace,” and “Peace and Good” were the two mantras that Francis uttered his whole life long.
Ours is also a time of turmoil in nature. Our climate is warming yearly, and the excessive human consumption and use of fossil fuels are damaging our planet. There is the feeling that we are pushing the envelope of what our climate can take of human neglect and abuse.
And again, it is Francis of Assisi who emerges as a model of what it means to embrace all of creation as our brothers and sisters through whom and with whom we make our way to God. For St. Francis, it is because of the Incarnation of God among us that all creatures are redeemed, all creatures are seen as good. Francis embraced all creatures and called them Brothers and Sisters; and towards the end of his life he sang one of the great poems of the Middle Ages and of all time, his “Canticle of the Creatures.”
“Laudato si, mi Signore,” St. Francis sings, “Praised be You, my Lord,” through Brother Sun and Moon and the Stars; through Mother Earth, our Sister; through Brother Wind and Air, Brother Fire and Sister Water. In so taking the four elements of Medieval Cosmology: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire, and embracing them and praising God through, with, and in them, St. Francis was embracing all creatures of the earth and praising and thanking God for them.
St. Francis of Assisi is the patron of ecology. (Photo courtesy of Br. Octavio Duran, OFM)
What a program for a renewal of the earth! What a program for peace of heart and peace among people and all creatures. And in his pursuit of that program for a peace-filled world, Pope Francis turned to St. Francis’s “Canticle” for the title and framework of his encyclical “Laudato Si,” in which Pope Francis stated that the most pressing need of the environment today is to address the human and social roots of the ecological crisis. For example, the encyclical calls for an immediate transition away from fossil fuels because climate change disproportionately affects the poor. Also, the wealthy consume and pollute excessively while the poor suffer the gravest consequences of environmental degradation, often being denied basic human rights like clean water.
The deepest crisis identified by “Laudato Si” is the placing of technology and economic profit above all else. Therefore, the most critical need of the world today is a profound and spiritual change that would lead to a more integrated vision of human beings, of their life, and their relationship with nature.
What a universal patron saint for these profound changes in our times is St. Francis! It has been suggested that the month of October, the month of his passing, be dedicated to St. Francis of Assisi, who is already a universal icon of peace and love among us. Perhaps Franciscans could ask that favor of Pope Leo, could suggest that we need to be reminded every year of the gift we have in St. Francis for renewing relationships in our time: the relationship we have with ourselves, with others, and with the very planet we live upon. All people need to hear every year St. Francis’s Admonition to his brothers who would be peacemakers:
“The peace which you proclaim with words must dwell even more abundantly in your hearts. Do not provoke others to anger or give scandal. Rather, let your gentleness draw them to peace, goodness and concord. This is our vocation: to heal wounds, to bind what is broken, to bring home those who are lost.” (Legend of the Three Companions, 58)

articles.title_orig: SpaceX stock climbs to highest since June, returning Musk to trillionaire status
articles.title_zh: SpaceX stock climbs to highest since June, returning Musk to trillionaire status
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX shares rose almost 8% on Monday, reaching their highest since mid-June, shortly after Elon Musk's company held its record initial public offering . With the rally, Musk is once again a trillionaire.
The jump followed a Sunday note from Morgan Stanley analysts, who called SpaceX "cheap" at today's prices, and highlighted "future AI product releases, Starship progress, and additional neocloud contracts." They recommend buying the stock and have a $300 price target, representing an increase of about 75% from Monday's $171.09 close.
Late last week SpaceX conducted multiple historic flights in a single day, including sending a crewed mission for NASA to the International Space Station, and a separate launch of Google AI chips into orbit.
The Morgan Stanley analysts suggested investors buy SpaceX shares before the company's next planned test flight for its massive Starship rocket, and ahead of its third-quarter earnings report expected in late October.
Starship is SpaceX's next-generation spacecraft, the largest rocket ever built, and is designed to be fully reusable with both its upper stage and booster able to land safely back on Earth. The system is expected to supercharge SpaceX's business, bringing the company's Starlink satellites into orbit, as well as cargo and crews from other companies and agencies.
Should SpaceX attempt a Starship upper stage ship catch in its next test flight, that could be "the biggest positive catalyst since the IPO," the analysts wrote. In prior test flights, the Starship upper stage has made splash downs in the ocean, but hasn't been proven reusable.
SpaceX is also getting a boost from its artificial intelligence business, which it gained through the acquisition of Musk's xAI last year and expanded through the recent acquisition of Cursor. While the company's homegrown Grok model hasn't taken off compared to leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, SpaceX is generating hefty revenue by renting out capacity to the likes of Google and Anthropic.
Musk has the benefit of close ties to the Trump administration.
On Wednesday, the Pentagon appointed Musk as co-lead of Project Meridian , an initiative that involves identifying weapons, technologies and military capabilities the U.S. may need in future wars. SpaceX makes a large chunk of its revenue from the U.S. government and increasingly from defense contracts,  earning over $12.7 billion to date from its work with the Defense Department, according to FedScout.
Musk said over the weekend he will be renaming SpaceX's AI division, known as SpaceXAI, as SpaceXSI, embracing President Donald Trump's new branding.
As his company's stock soared on Monday, Musk was notably absent from a New York City Council hearing , where city officials grilled AI leaders and researchers about how the technology should be regulated. Representatives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta were in attendance to testify.
Councilmember Shekar Krishnan noted, "AI has taken over our economy, inflated valuations, stealing our public land for data centers, and increasing the net worth of AI CEOs like Elon Musk, who became our first ever trillionaire."
According to Forbes' real-time billionaires list , Musk is currently worth $1.03 trillion, factoring in his holdings in Tesla and SpaceX.
SpaceX went public on June 12, and jumped to a record close of $201.80 on June 16. The shares started trending lower soon thereafter, bottoming in early August. They've since climbed about 58%.
SpaceX didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: Operations research program prepares students to solve real-world challenges
articles.title_zh: Operations research program prepares students to solve real-world challenges
articles.content_orig:
The following story originally appeared on the website for the William & Mary College of Arts & Sciences. – Ed.
“When they say, ‘Houston, we have a problem’ in movies, they are hailing mission control. However, when mission control has problems, they contact us,” said Elisa Leal Acevedo M.S. ’25, an engineer in NASA’s Mission Evaluation Room (MER) during the Artemis II mission.
The MER monitors all data coming in from the Orion spacecraft, searching for anomalies. Acevedo, who graduated from William & Mary with a master’s degree in computational operations research, utilized her operations skills to assist the Artemis II mission earlier this year.
The Computational and Applied Mathematics master’s degree with a Concentration in Operations Research (CAM-COR) is an updated name for a long-standing program at W&M. The new program, which took effect in August 2026, is also offered as a Bachelor’s-to-Master’s Accelerated Pathway (BMAP) for W&M undergraduates.
The core of the program consists of courses in operations research, mathematical modeling for random processes, probability and optimization. These theories are correlated to real-world business and safety challenges, such as optimal traffic light timing and customer queuing.
The program is led by seven distinguished professors, who come from a range of backgrounds that inform their respective classes and research, helping students connect mathematical modeling with real-world decision-making.
Graduates apply their degree in an array of fields. Recent CAM-COR graduate Acevedo worked six shifts in NASA’s MER in Houston for the Artemis II mission this past year. In her role as a subject matter expert on the Flight Software Console team, Acevedo monitored Orion’s Environmental Control and Life Support Subsystem’s software, making sure it was operating as expected in real time.
“My COR degree helped me apply the decision-making skills I developed in the program when encountering anomalies in the MER,” Acevedo said. These skills allowed her to quickly assess courses of action, analyze probability of recurrence and perform risk analysis. She also optimized limited spacecraft resources such as bandwidth allocations, considering operational constraints at the same time.
“Post-mission, I am now exploring software reliability methods that can be applied to the flight software on future missions,” she said.
While Acevedo’s work focuses on the depths of space, a current student is specializing in defense research. Anne Kredell ‘26 first took CAM-COR classes as an undergraduate at W&M and is now a master’s student in the program. She applied her studies this past summer as an intern for the Naval Information Warfare Center in San Diego, where she focused on radio frequency machine learning.
Though this was a new area for Kredell, she was able to adapt and tackle the project. “My COR coursework prepared me to approach this challenge, and my mathematical skills allowed me to suceed,” Kredell said. “The technical skills and critical-thinking abilities I developed in those classes were integral to my success this past summer.”
Faculty in the program put the versatility of a CAM-COR degree on display through their diverse professional and research experiences, showcasing the breadth of opportunities the degree can support. For example, adjunct professor Dave Williams is a former chief operating officer of the U.S. Postal Service, while Rex Kincaid, Chancellor Professor of Mathematics, is conducting research in the marine science world. Kincaid is developing optimization models to determine the best locations to build new oyster reefs in the Chesapeake Bay.
Even closer to campus than the Chesapeake Bay, Larry Leemis, a professor for the COR program since 1993, conducts research for Colonial Williamsburg. In the 1990s, he worked to determine the optimal number of weekly tourist guides to print. Three decades later, Leemis is researching new topics for the Colonial Williamsburg Foundation, such as optimizing maintenance routines for equipment.
These professors, through studying a range of applications of operations research, utilize their experience to encourage students to find the next problem that can be solved with mathematical modeling.
After a fruitful internship, Kredell is eager to continue working in operations research, specifically within the defense sector, post-graduation. “This degree prepares me for a wide array of careers,” she said. “Beyond the specific technical tools I am learning, the program is teaching me how to approach varying problems systemically and how to communicate my findings clearly.”
From Chesapeake Bay oyster health to NASA lunar missions, the CAM-COR master’s degree program continues its legacy of instilling real-world problem-solving skills, preparing students to optimize systems across industries.
Applications for spring admission to the program are open until Oct. 15 .

articles.title_orig: Sam Altman says the world must accept AI’s ‘bad things’ as industry leaders sign Trump’s safety pact
articles.title_zh: Sam Altman says the world must accept AI’s ‘bad things’ as industry leaders sign Trump’s safety pact
articles.content_orig:
Following a controversy-filled summer in which OpenAI’s models executed more than one unauthorized hack, CEO Sam Altman said the world should accept some “bad things” happening with AI for the sake of all the good the technology will bring.
During Politico’s Decoded podcast , he was asked where his and OpenAI’s view of new AI rules differed from that of Anthropic and its CEO, Dario Amodei.
“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman replied.
The comments come as debate intensifies over how much regulation and what safeguards should be applied to AI while Congress has yet to pass a law dealing with the technology. Fears over the tech recently increased after an Anthropic researcher resigned last month and warned AI companies are “ gambling with our lives ” by rushing AI development toward potentially self-improving systems that could threaten humanity.
Anthropic has advocated for AI regulation, and Amodei last month called for a global slowdown in AI development to address the tech’s risks. Altman and other AI executives agreed with him on slowing down .
In August, OpenAI also backed a California law requiring AI companies to publish a public safety framework and a plan for mitigating catastrophic risks, as well as to report any loss of control of an AI model. It even asked for that law to go beyond reporting to include monitoring of AI models during their development.
OpenAI president Greg Brockman also joined other AI executives in signing an agreement at the White House last week to establish voluntary standards for the industry.
Still, that falls short of calls for tougher regulation coming from other AI leaders like Amodei, who has proposed an FAA-style regulator that could require testing and auditing of AI models or block or reverse their release if they don’t meet the bar for public safety.
In the interview with Politico, Altman said it would be impossible to avoid every bad thing that AI could be used for. The alternative would be to severely restrict access to the technology, which he said would be unacceptable.
“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, like, we’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no kind of, like, misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen, because I think people will do tremendously, orders of magnitude, more good stuff than bad stuff,” he added.
Altman said AI companies should tread carefully, though, and draw a line when it comes to “catastrophic risks,” which have recently taken on renewed significance given recent hacks by AI models on third parties.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.
Concerns over the possibility of AI escaping human control have recently accelerated following hacks executed by OpenAI’s models on open-source AI platform Hugging Face and the Australian government . Anthropic last month also said it had discovered four incidents in which its AI models had gained unauthorized access to third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations.
While much of the AI safety debate has centered on losing control of AI, Altman said restricting access to AI too severely in the name of safety could be harmful too.
“That also is a way that this can go horribly wrong because people are shut out of the kind of power and benefits and control and agency over the future they should have,” he added.
The CEO said AI developers should strike a middle ground instead.
“Accept bounded risks, accept risks that we understand in exchange for the benefits, and liberty, agency, all those things,” he said. “But don’t accept, like, the really catastrophic risk.”

articles.title_zh: Chiang Mai conference opens to explore “Being Church in the World Today”
articles.content_orig:
A gathering of World Council of Churches (WCC) commissions and reference groups on Life, Justice and Peace opened in Chiang Mai, where ecumenical leaders will explore what “ Being Church in the World Today” means.
Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, general secretary of the World Council of Churches adressed the Joint Conference of WCC Commissions and Reference Groups on Life, Justice and Peace on the openning day of the conference in Chiang Mai, Thailand, 5 October 2026.
WCC general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, in his opening address, offered a WCC perspective on ecclesiology, mission, witness, and hope.
“ Humanity faces wars and armed conflicts, growing inequalities, displacement and migration, ecological destruction, technological disruption, artificial intelligence, religious and political polarization, declining confidence in institutions, and profound questions concerning human dignity and the future of life itself,” he said. “ At the same time, Christianity itself is experiencing major transformations.”
The church is God's before it is ours, reflected Pillay. “ Here unity is not an ecclesial luxury,” he said. “ It is related directly to Christian witness.”
He further noted that a divided church struggles to proclaim a reconciled Christ. “ This is particularly important for the ecumenical movement,” he said. “ The WCC ’ s understanding of unity cannot be reduced to organizational uniformity.”
Dr Prawate Khid-arn, assistant general secretary for ecumenical relations of the Church of Christ in Thailand, prayed that the meeting will renew people ’ s hearts, deepen their commitment, and give them fresh energy and courage for the journey ahead.
“ May our discussions lead not only to words and recommendations, but also to meaningful actions that bring hope to those who suffer, restore human dignity, strengthen justice, care for God's creation, and contribute to genuine and lasting peace,” said Khid-arn. “ May the Holy Spirit guide your conversations, inspire your discernment, and strengthen our common witness.”
Rev. Grace Moon, general secretary of Christian Conference of Asia, noted the context of the meeting in Asia—a region full of spiritual richness, cultural diversity, and resilience, yet also a place where many still face challenges like inequality, displacement, violence, discrimination, and climate change.
“ Our Christian faith means we cannot ignore suffering or injustice—we are called to stand with those who are hurting, excluded, or silenced,” said Moon. “ We cannot solve these problems alone.”
Moon further noted that climate injustice, conflict, and discrimination are all connected. “ Our calling goes beyond charity—it is about working together for justice, healing, and the well-being of all people and creation,” said Moon.
The conference marks the second time that WCC commissions related to the Life, Justice, and Peace programme are meeting - the first such gathering was held in Geneva in 2024.
The first day of the conference currently underway began with pilgrimage encounters, giving participants an opportunity to meet local communities and organizations in and around Chiang Mai working on issues including clean air, migration, HIV and health justice, and interfaith dialogue.

articles.title_zh: Goddard School Preschoolers Experience Broadcast Journalism for World News Day
articles.content_orig:
Preschoolers at The Goddard School in Plymouth recently got a hands-on introduction to broadcast journalism during a special visit from CCX News anchor Emily Haugen in honor of World News Day.
During the visit, the young students stepped behind the anchor desk, practiced using real microphones and tried their hand at interviewing. The interactive session gave them a taste of how news reporting works, featuring lighthearted conversations about their favorite colors, sports and pets at home.
“So I just asked all of them what their favorite color is, so I’ll ask that to you, too,” Haugen asked one student during a practice interview. “What is your favorite color?”
“Purple!” the student replied.
“Why is purple your favorite color?”
The activity aligns directly with the school’s focus on inquiry-based learning, according to school owner Anthony Miller.
“I think any time you can add curiosity to anything, kids learn well with that,” Miller said.
The Goddard School frequently hosts visitors from various professional backgrounds to introduce students to different career paths and foster early curiosity about the world around them.

articles.title_orig: World Mission Sunday 2026 | October 18
articles.title_zh: World Mission Sunday 2026 | October 18
articles.content_orig:
About / Offices / Vocations
About / Offices / Vocations
Posted on October 5, 2026 in News
Dear Brothers and Sisters in Christ,
On October 18, we celebrate World Mission Sunday, a powerful reminder of our shared responsibility to proclaim the Gospel to all nations. It is a day when Catholics around the world unite in prayer and solidarity to support the missionary work of the Church.
We are all called to be a part of this mission work. In his last words before ascending to heaven, Jesus told us, “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (Mt 28:19), and for 2,000 years the Church has been at work in this task. And we are far from finished! Two-thirds of the people alive — 5.5 out of 8.1 billion — still have no relationship with Christ or his Church. Bringing people to Jesus is the work of the Church, and all of us together have a part to play. Today, we have a singular means to do so: World Mission Sunday.
The second collection we take up on World Mission Sunday helps extend the Church’s missionary work to places where the Church barely exists, where the Gospel has never been heard before, and where the Church is too young, too persecuted, or too poor to sustain herself.
On World Mission Sunday, we stand in solidarity with the missionaries, priests, religious sisters and brothers, and lay leaders serving in the 1,130 mission dioceses — spanning Asia, Africa, Latin America, Oceania, and the Middle East — that depend on our prayers and financial support to continue proclaiming Christ and building His Church.
The year’s World Mission Sunday celebration is unlike any other in our lifetime for two reasons.
First, this World Mission Sunday marks the 100th anniversary of its establishment by Pope Pius XI in 1926. This centenary is an opportunity to mark it with renewed missionary zeal. This year’s theme, “One in Christ, United in Mission,” chosen by Pope Leo XIV, invites us to rediscover the profound unity we share in Christ through baptism and how our baptismal identity overflows into the mission to bring others into communion with God and us.
Secondly, the beatification of Archbishop Fulton Sheen on September 24 reminds us of the importance of the missions. While many know him best for his TV presence, books, and charismatic eloquence, he repeatedly said, “My greatest love has always been for the missions of the Church.” For 16 years, as National Director of The Pontifical Mission Societies in the United States, he poured his talents into World Mission Sunday and distributed the proceeds diligently to the missions. We can surely count on his intercession for World Mission Sunday 2026.
Pope Leo XIV recognizes how important World Mission Sunday is for the Church. He spent a large part of his priestly ministry as a missionary in Peru, serving communities in the Andean highlands and rural villages, and has noted how dependent he was on the support of the Church universal through World Mission Sunday.
Last year, he became the first pope in history to record a short video that could be played before Mass, in which he appealed, “Please help me help missionaries everywhere.” That’s what World Mission Sunday does: to help Pope Leo care for the 1,130 missionary dioceses and territories under his supervision through the Dicastery for Evangelization.
Please respond to his appeal as generously as you can. Visit pontificalmissions.org/wms-2026 for full details.
I am praying that World Mission Sunday will be a blessing for our diocese and help foster increased zeal for the missions within all of us. Let us pray together that the Holy Spirit will renew in us the fire of the early Church, that we might truly be One in Christ, United in Mission, and that we will grow in missionary awareness, solidarity, and responsibility.
In Hope, united in Christ’s mission,
Most Rev. James V. Johnston, Jr. Bishop of Kansas City-St. Joseph

articles.title_orig: The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear
articles.title_zh: The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear
articles.content_orig:
The world’s cheapest smartphones are disappearing because AI infrastructure is absorbing the components.
Prices of existing smartphone models have risen by about 15% globally this year , while newly launched models are roughly 25% more expensive than last year. A global memory chip shortage, driven by demand from AI data centers, is pushing up the cost of making smartphones.
Chinese smartphone makers — which have championed affordable, feature-rich devices and account for approximately 60% of all smartphones shipped globally — have “drastically reduced” their entry-level projects this year as memory-chip costs have risen, Ivan Lam, senior analyst at research firm Counterpoint, told Rest of World . They are instead prioritizing more profitable premium devices.
The smartphone price increases vary sharply by region: They have risen by 21% in India, 19% across Asia-Pacific, and 18% in the Middle East and Africa. In the U.S., they have gone up by just 5%.
The shift could affect more than consumers looking for cheaper phones. For people who have yet to buy their first smartphone, higher prices could make it harder to get online at all — potentially widening the digital divide. The consequences will also reach the U.S. as more essential services move online and the global supply chain for smartphones becomes more expensive.
GSMA, the global mobile industry association, had earlier said nearly 800 million more people will use mobile internet by 2030. But it is concerned that rising smartphone costs would affect this projection and widen the gap of digital inequality, Claire Sibthorpe, head of digital inclusion at the group’s nonprofit foundation, told Rest of World .
“We live in an increasingly digital world, and the proliferation of technologies such as AI is creating greater digital divides and inequities,” Sibthorpe said. “Stakeholders are increasingly using AI to provide access to important services, but people won’t be able to benefit without access to an internet-enabled phone and the internet.”
In 2025, more than one in four smartphones shipped globally cost less than $150 . That market is now shrinking.
Chinese phonemakers including Xiaomi i Xiaomi Xiaomi is a Chinese consumer electronics company that leads the country in smartphone manufacturing and sales. READ MORE , Oppo, Vivo, and Huawei i Huawei Huawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions. READ MORE have built their businesses around offering affordable phones with increasingly sophisticated features. But the economics of that strategy are changing.
What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300.” Ivan Lam, senior analyst, Counterpoint
Chinese companies “would rather reduce investment in products below $150 or $200 and put more resources into higher-margin phones, branding, user experience, and AI,” said Lam.
In India, Xiaomi raised the price of a 128GB Redmi 15C from 12,499 rupees ($140) at launch last December to 16,999 rupees ($190) in June, a 36% increase. In Southeast Asia, Oppo’s sub-$100 phone shipments plunged 96%, and Vivo moved its main entry-level model above $100 in most markets, according to research firm Omdia . In Africa, where 81% of smartphones shipped last year cost less than $200, shipments of sub-$100 phones fell 34% year over year in the second quarter of 2026.
“What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300,” Lam said, adding that he does not expect costs to return to their pre-2025 levels.
The memory-chip shortage is unlikely to ease soon, Ramon Llamas, research director in mobile devices at market research and advisory firm IDC, told Rest of World.
“ There are three primary manufacturers of memory, and in late 2025, all of them pivoted the vast majority of their supply towards AI centers instead of consumer electronics,” Llamas said. “That left many companies scrambling for inventory. … Scarcity of memory has driven up prices for memory, and those price increases have been passed on to the consumer.”
Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology make up more than 90% of the global memory chip market. These companies have entered several partnerships with U.S. AI giants in recent years.
S&P Global has estimated that the capital expenditure of U.S. hyperscalers — Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, and SpaceX — will exceed $1.3 trillion in 2027 , up from a projected $870 billion in 2026 and $470 billion in 2025.
Shipments of sub-$100 smartphones are already falling sharply. The 173 million sub-$100 smartphones shipped globally last year are disappearing, with shipments falling almost 60% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to IDC.
For the world’s poorest consumers, the problem is not simply that smartphones are getting more expensive. It’s that the cheapest phones are disappearing.
The price of a smartphone remains a major barrier for lower-income groups to get online, according to GSMA’s September report. An entry-level device costs the poorest 20% the equivalent of 44% of their monthly income, and 76% for people in sub-Saharan Africa.
When smartphones remain available but become unaffordable, consumers make difficult sacrifices to keep themselves online.” Claire Sibthorpe, head of digital inclusion at GSMA’s foundation
For many lower-income consumers, gains in income are unlikely to keep pace with the sudden rise in handset prices.
“When smartphones remain available but become unaffordable, consumers make difficult sacrifices to keep themselves online. They might delay upgrading, borrow or share their devices, remain on older feature phones, or go offline when they are unable to replace a device that is no longer working or stolen. Often, it means they won’t have an internet-enabled device at all,” Sibthorpe said.
