Global terminal operator DP World has taken another step toward returning to U.S. port operations two decades after a proposed takeover of terminals at several major American ports raised concerns over national security.
The Port of Corpus Christi, Texas, has signed a lease option agreement with Dubai-based DP World to develop a container terminal capable of eventually handling about 1 million twenty-foot equivalent units annually, according to a port official.
“We’ve signed a lease option agreement with DP World for a development … of a container terminal in the Port,” Jeffrey Pollack, chief strategy and sustainability officer for the Port of Corpus Christi Authority, told the American Journal of Transportation during the American Association of Port Authorities annual convention in New Orleans on Sept. 29.
Corpus Christi currently is not a container port, and Pollack said adding container operations would significantly diversify a cargo base heavily centered on energy.
Pollack said officials envision a relatively modest container operation by the standards of the largest U.S. gateways, with capacity ultimately topping out around 1 million TEUs annually.
The agreement represents a significant potential return to U.S. marine terminal operations for DP World.
The company, which is owned by the government of Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, became the center of a major political controversy in 2006 after its acquisition of British terminal operator P&O would have transferred P&O’s terminal leases and operations at several major U.S. ports to DP World.
The deal triggered bipartisan opposition in Congress over national security concerns and ultimately led DP World to divest P&O’s U.S. port operations, according to the U.S. Senate Commerce Committee’s Feb. 28, 2006 hearing, “Security of Terminal Operations at U.S. Ports.”
DP World ultimately announced in March 2006 that it would divest P&O’s U.S. operations after lawmakers moved to block the transaction. The controversy came despite the George W. Bush administration’s support for the transaction and its position that port security would remain under the responsibility of U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Coast Guard.
The Corpus Christi project would mark DP World’s first U.S. container terminal development since that episode and its first container terminal development on the U.S. Gulf Coast.
DP World is one of the world’s largest terminal operators, handling roughly 10% of global container traffic through more than 60 ports and terminals.
DP World and the Port of Corpus Christi first announced in June that they had entered exclusive negotiations for a long-term lease. Under the proposed development, DP World would design, build and operate the terminal.
At the time, the parties said negotiations would focus on terminal design, capacity planning and the project’s investment structure.
The project could significantly alter Corpus Christi’s position in Gulf Coast freight markets.
The port is one of the nation’s largest gateways by total tonnage but has historically focused on crude oil, liquefied natural gas, refined petroleum products, agricultural commodities and industrial cargo rather than containers.
Corpus Christi also recently acquired about 2,000 acres roughly 8 to 10 miles south of its Inner Harbor that port officials envision as an inland port supporting the proposed container terminal.
Pollack said the property can connect with all three Class I railroads serving the port and multiple interstate highway systems, potentially attracting manufacturing, warehousing and other import-export operations.
The container push comes as Corpus Christi continues posting record overall cargo volumes. Customers moved 110.3 million tons through the Corpus Christi Ship Channel during the first half of 2026, up 7.7% from the previous first-half record of 102.4 million tons set a year earlier.
Why it matters: The project at the Port of Corpus Christi, Texas, would bring DP World back into U.S. container terminal operations two decades after national security concerns in Congress derailed its acquisition of terminal operations at several major American ports.

articles.title_orig: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.title_zh: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.content_orig:
Wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse and its numbers dwindled across New Zealand due to predators and habitat loss
The population of New Zealand’s endemic wētāpunga – believed to be the world’s heaviest insect – is officially “increasing” thanks to a groundbreaking breeding programme that has overseen the release of 11,000 insects into the wild.
“The future of wētāpunga is looking bright,” said Dr Chris Green, an honorary researcher at the department of conservation, who documented the success of the project for the New Zealand Journal of Zoology. Green co-authored a report released on 2 October that outlines the success of the breeding programme.
“Eleven thousand individuals for release is extraordinary and outstanding.”
A female wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse. Its body can grow up to 10cm long (nearly 4in) and its leg span can be as wide as 20cm.
It is the largest of 70 wētā species and was once found across parts of the North Island before predation from introduced species and habitat loss contributed to their decline. By the 1990s, they were considered “endangered” and are now presumed extinct in the wild on New Zealand’s mainland. The insects reside primarily on a smattering of predator-free islands in Auckland’s Hauraki Gulf and off the coast of Northland.
But their fortune is starting to change. Over the past 15 years, tens of thousands of wētāpunga have been bred at Butterfly Creek, a wildlife facility, and Auckland zoo, enabling the release of wētāpunga across new predator-free islands and some mainland reserves north of Auckland.
Butterfly Creek and Auckland zoo established husbandry techniques that, over time, have been scaled up to rear large numbers of wētāpunga in communal creches. The young wētāpunga – or nymphs – are fed a three-part diet of fresh foliage, fish flake protein and leaf litter. The protein is “critical” to the survival of the youngest nymphs, Green said.
Once big enough to protect themselves, the insects are transferred to their new habitat. The efforts have led to 45 separate translocations to wild habitats, which is “a very high number in any recovery of a species”, Green said.
Monitoring on two islands has shown wētāpunga have established self-sustaining populations, with fourth and fifth generations born there, in what Green said was a marker of success. As a result, the species’ conservation status has improved from “nationally endangered” to “nationally increasing”.
“It’s so exciting, because we are unable to report that for so many of our other threatened species,” Green said.
New Zealand is particularly vulnerable to species decline because of its high rates of endemism and problems with introduced pests.
Green said the country was at the forefront of invertebrate recovery work and he was not aware of any other examples of breeding programmes working to this scale, or with such success.
By documenting the project’s work, he hopes other institutions will feel encouraged to develop their own programmes.
“That’s the extraordinary aspect of it – that we’ve been successful,” he said. “If other institutions can get into that sort of position, then there can be huge benefit for threatened species in New Zealand.”

articles.title_orig: Pre-COP31: World Leaders Must Show Up for the Pacific Through Action, Not Just Speeches
articles.title_zh: Pre-COP31: World Leaders Must Show Up for the Pacific Through Action, Not Just Speeches
articles.content_orig:
As Pacific leaders, communities and civil society gather in Fiji and Tuvalu for the Pre-COP31 meetings, the expected absence of many world leaders must not become another excuse for climate inaction, Amnesty International said today.
The meetings come after an unusually hot European summer, with August 2026 becoming the joint-hottest month on record. Against the looming threat of a powerful El Niño, widespread wildfires, droughts, and floods, the new UN warning of the world rapidly breaching warming thresholds adds urgency to the need for decisive climate action.
“World leaders have spent years talking about the climate threats facing the Pacific. Now they must come to Fiji and Tuvalu, listen to Pacific communities and act. Rising seas are already eating away at people’s lands, livelihoods and cultures. Concern without action will not hold back the tide,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“Those who do not show up in person cannot evade their responsibilities. Their absence will not stop the seas from rising or erase the obligations of high-emitting countries towards communities paying the highest price for a crisis they did least to cause.
“An empty seat is not the greatest failure. The greater failure is an empty promise. Pre-COP31 must turn years of rhetoric into concrete commitments and action that deliver the climate ambition the world needs at COP31 in November.”
Fiji’s Environment Minister has said that the Pacific-led summit will proceed “with or without” major world leaders .
The Pacific is sounding the alarm
Amnesty International has documented how climate change is already harming human rights in Tuvalu, Kiribati and other Pacific Island countries . Rising seas, extreme heat, droughts and saltwater intrusion are threatening people’s rights to water, food, health, adequate housing and a safe future. Tuvalu contributes less than 0.003% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet it faces some of the climate crisis’ most severe consequences.
During her visit to Tuvalu in 2025, Agnès Callamard witnessed efforts by communities and the authorities to reclaim land from the advancing sea and enable people to remain in their homeland.
“To any world leader who hesitates to confront the biggest crisis of our time, I say this: come to Tuvalu. Speak to people living with rising seas and extreme heat. Witness their daily struggle to adapt, protect their rights and push back against the impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause. The reclaimed land in Tuvalu is not a tourist backdrop. It represents a country fighting for its survival,” said Agnès Callamard.
Students from the Pacific took the fight against climate change to the world’s top court, leading the International Court of Justice to issue a landmark Advisory Opinion in July 2025, which made it clear that governments have a legal obligation to protect human rights from climate change impacts.
“The Pacific should not have to plead for the world’s attention. Climate action is no longer simply a political choice. It is a legal and moral imperative,” said Agnès Callamard.
“Governments must end fossil fuel use and expansion through just transitions that leave no one behind, tax big polluters and deliver scaled up grants-based climate finance, providing climate reparations and ensuring communities on the front lines of the climate crisis have the resources and power to determine their own futures. The Pacific is sounding the alarm. If the world fails to act here, it will fail everywhere.”
Australia must turn partnership into action
As President of Negotiations at COP31, Australia has a particular responsibility to stand with its Pacific neighbors and secure an ambitious, human rights-centered outcome. Australia cannot credibly claim climate leadership while continuing to support fossil fuel expansion that deepens the harms facing Pacific communities.
Based on Amnesty International’s recommendations ahead of COP31 , Australia and other governments must use pre-COP31 to advance three priorities:
“Pacific leadership has helped keep the fight for 1.5°C alive, but Pacific communities cannot carry the burden of global climate leadership alone,” said Agnès Callamard. “Australia must use its presiding role to turn Pacific demands into COP31 outcomes, starting with stopping the crisis at source through a just transition away from fossil fuels.”
No climate justice without environmental defenders
Governments cannot deliver climate justice while excluding affected communities or silencing those who challenge harmful projects. Across the world, Indigenous Peoples, environmental human rights defenders and communities on the front lines of the climate crisis are resisting fossil fuel expansion and fighting for fairer, more sustainable futures. Yet many face harassment, surveillance, criminalization, violence and restrictions on peaceful protest.
Australia’s treatment of peaceful climate activists will be an important test of its climate leadership. There are also concerns about restrictions on freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly in Fiji.
Ahead of COP31, Amnesty International is launching a global campaign “Protecting our Future: Environmental Human Rights Defenders Powering Just Transitions” spotlighting environmental human rights defenders and the alternatives they are fighting for around the world. This includes the First Nations people in Australia, who are challenging offshore oil and gas exploration affecting their lands and waters.
The campaign will show what resistance, dignity and a people-powered just transition can look like when communities refuse to see their lands, waters and futures sacrificed for fossil fuel profits.
Australia and Fiji must ensure that civil society, Indigenous Peoples, affected communities and environmental defenders can participate, speak out and protest peacefully without discrimination, intimidation or reprisals.
“Environmental defenders are protecting our shared future. Governments must listen to them, protect them and ensure they have a meaningful say in climate decisions,” said Agnès Callamard.
“COP31 must deliver more than promises. Anything less would betray our shared responsibility to uphold human rights and secure climate justice.”

articles.title_orig: How the Nike x ‘One Piece’ Collaboration Joined the Lore-Filled World — NIKE, Inc.
articles.title_zh: How the Nike x ‘One Piece’ Collaboration Joined the Lore-Filled World — NIKE, Inc.
articles.content_orig:
Since it initially published in 1997, the Japanese manga series ONE PIECE has surpassed 600 million copies in its circulation, on par with the biggest superhero comics and most popular wizarding-world books. To call creator Eiichiro Oda’s series a cultural behemoth would be like calling ONE PIECE ’s legendary “Blue Sea” a mere body of water — technically true, but wildly short of it.
Dr. B’s Research Lab at Nike’s Harajuku pop-up, recasting Bill Bowerman as a scientist studying the Devil Fruit–inspired Air Max Plus collabs. Here, the three models hang suspended like specimens.
You can call it manifest destiny that the world’s most popular manga and the world’s largest sports company would join forces at some point . But for Nike to honor the legacy of a pop culture landmark so robust and influential that fans literally name their children after characters, it couldn’t just be a simple merch collaboration. Instead, Nike answered with three Air Max Plus silhouettes, each inspired by a Devil Fruit (from ONE PIECE lore), apparel stitched with references only the faithful will catch, and a globe-trotting rollout meant to be explored like the story it came from. With a mythology this deep and only one shot to engage with the canon, Nike Virtual Studios’ .SWOOSH team knew it had to come correct.
“When a brand collabs with ‘ONE PIECE,’ they are creating something new for the community; they are adding to the incredibly rich lore of the story.”
“When a brand collabs with ONE PIECE , they are creating something new for the community; they are adding to the incredibly rich lore of the story,” says Ashwin Shinde, .SWOOSH's Senior Manager, Energy Gaming Product Merch on Nike’s ONE PIECE Collection. “So, we lean on the thing that’s always going to set us apart from other brands. What is a story that only Nike could tell?”
For .SWOOSH, the answer started with a conceptual parallel. “We took the spirit of Nike and its desire to push people beyond their human potential and combined it with the Devil Fruits, which literally give people the ability to go beyond human potential and essentially have superpowers,” says Bryce Wong, Senior Manager, Gaming Footwear Product Design.
Bridging the two brand universes, the team landed on a single idea: “If Devil Fruits existed in our world, they would be Nikes.” From there, the task became choosing the right shoe to bring it to life. Wong proposed the Air Max Plus, an iconic model whose expressive cage and dimensional upper made it, in the words of Senior Designer Yuchung Chen, “a perfect design to blend with the whimsical world of ONE PIECE .”
Translating a superpower-inducing fruit into the shoe meant reworking every surface. “Each Devil Fruit design posed its own challenge of maintaining the motion and directionality of the original shoe’s cage design while keeping it light and open,” says Chen, who wrapped the fruit pattern across the mudguard, cage and shank. Each upper got its own finish: gummy and rubber-like for Gum Gum, a velvety peach-fuzz for Ope Ope, and an on-fire sunset for Mera Mera that nods to the OG Air Max Plus.
The deepest cut is on the medial shank: a contrasting color bites a chunk clean out, a reference to the panel where rubber-limbed hero Monkey D. Luffy accidentally eats the Gum Gum fruit — or, as Chen noted in a wink for the heads, it has another, real name — thinking of it as dessert.
“We took the spirit of Nike and its desire to push people beyond their human potential and combined it with the Devil
Fruits, which literally give people the ability to go beyond human potential. If Devil Fruits existed
in our world, they would be Nikes.”
The apparel scaled the same logic up: mythical fruit into tangible object, rendered on fabric. “Following that same approach, the patterns, colors and textures of the Devil Fruits that inspired the footwear are enlarged and abstracted into layered graphics,” explains Lead, Global Brand Digital Designer, Sarah Kim. This makes each piece a “wearable abstraction of the shoes and, by extension, the fruits themselves.”
She built the graphic tees around Laboon — the whale character who waits years for the promised return of his old friends, making a promise with Luffy  — because of the way his endurance speaks to both sides of the collab at once. “We wanted the choices to ultimately communicate the shared ethos of a Nike athlete and a shonen manga hero: resilience, perseverance and the ability to keep going.”
The building takeover in Shanghai, including a Straw Hats’ Jolly Roger reworked with a Swoosh for crossbones, beside a flaming “WANT ’EM” ad wrapping the space.
The team also used canonical deep cuts to inject the collaboration with inside jokes that will make loyalists salivate. This includes a vest that nods to one of the manga’s core rules, that Devil Fruit consumers trade their ability to swim for their powers. “The vest was an addition that emerged as a meta and cheeky way to play into the lore as we got deeper into development and more immersed in the ONE PIECE universe,” says Kim.
Inside Dr. B’s Research Lab, including the “hated by the sea” vest.
The same investment into authenticity even shaped the release’s packaging. Open the shoebox and your reflection stares back from a “Wanted” poster printed inside, casting buyers as pirates with bounties on their heads, like so many of the ONE PIECE heroes. “The idea behind the mirror was to make the person opening the box part of the story,” says Global Brand Experience Designer Heena Chung. “Your reflection completes the poster and, for a second, you become part of the ONE PIECE world.” She designed the packaging as a “treasure chest” with a staged reveal, down to a reward for completists: line up all three boxes and the Devil Fruit graphics connect into a single panoramic artwork.
The unboxing was intentionally designed to unfold in stages, like a treasure chest built to reveal itself over time. Printed tissue gives way to a trading card; the shoes wait beneath as the prize.
Between the lid and the shoes, printed tissue paper hides its own ONE PIECE iconography. “There’s a deliberate progression to the reveal,” says Chung. “The exterior establishes the collaboration, the tissue introduces another layer of the world, and the mirror creates the final interaction by placing you directly inside the Wanted poster.”
The IYKYK references are dense and intentional, but they aren’t the raison d'être. “The bigger goal was to capture the feeling of ONE PIECE rather than simply collect Easter eggs,” says Chung. “The box becomes part of the collaboration itself — something worth keeping and exploring rather than just a container for the product.”
“The bigger goal was to capture the feeling of ‘ONE PIECE’ rather than simply collect Easter eggs.”
A collection this considered could have simply dropped, no problem. Instead, the deep bench of the global .SWOOSH team took it off the shelf and into the wild by staging physical activations across nearly two dozen cities worldwide, turning the release into something fans can travel to and track down. The blueprint came straight from the source. ”“Creatively, the table was already set by Oda’s story of the ONE PIECE protagonist and his crew, known as the Straw Hats, traveling the world and searching for treasure,” says Wong. “We wanted to parallel that with the world of sneaker collecting, giving people a reason to find their crew, discover, and experience something different along the way.”
Dr. B’s mobile lab, parked in Harajuku and rigged out. Nike’s answer to Dr. Vegapunk, the ‘ONE PIECE’ scientist who studies the Devil Fruits.
That hunt materialized city by city. In the Harajuku district of Tokyo, a Nike-branded Poneglyph — one of the manga’s ancient, indestructible tablets inscribed in a lost language — appeared on Cat Street, teasing the release with no explanation unless you’re fluent in the saga. Below the Nike store there, the team built out Dr. B’s Research Lab, a nod to Dr. Vegap

Getting to space is no longer just a matter of building a rocket and launching it once. Reusable boosters, new launch vehicles and a growing commercial space industry are reshaping the path to orbit — a transformation that will take center stage during this year's World Space Week.
World Space Week (WSW) 2026 runs from Oct. 4 through Oct. 10, with this year's theme, "Rocket Revolution," highlighting the technologies and organizations changing how humanity reaches and uses space. The global celebration brings together space agencies, companies, educators, students, museums, astronomy clubs and space enthusiasts for events and activities around the world.
The annual celebration of WSW is tied to two important milestones in spaceflight history. Oct. 4 marks the anniversary of the 1957 launch of Sputnik 1 , the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth, while Oct. 10 marks the signing of the Outer Space Treaty in 1967, which established principles for the peaceful exploration and use of outer space. The United Nations General Assembly established WSW as an annual observance in 1999.
This year's theme "recognizes how increased space access and falling launch prices have stimulated the space ecosystem and exciting new space applications," Dennis Stone, WSW Association president, said in a statement from the organization, adding that the theme is also intended to inspire student interest in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, or STEM.
For decades, reaching orbit required enormous amounts of hardware, fuel and infrastructure — and rockets were generally designed to fly only once. That model has increasingly begun to change.
Reusable rockets have demonstrated that portions of a launch vehicle can return to Earth and fly again, while a growing number of commercial companies and countries are developing new ways to put satellites, spacecraft and other payloads into orbit.
The change is about more than simply building bigger or more powerful rockets . Reusability and new launch architectures could alter the economics and cadence of spaceflight, while smaller launch vehicles are opening additional options for organizations looking to send spacecraft into orbit.
The result is a space industry with more participants and a wider range of missions — from communications and Earth-observation satellites to scientific spacecraft and human spaceflight. Just last month, SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time during its Sept. 28 test flight , successfully deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites in a major milestone for the vehicle's development. The mission was ultimately cut short after an engine issue, but achieved its primary objectives of reaching orbit and deploying its payload.
More frequent and diverse access to orbit supports an expanding ecosystem of satellites and spacecraft that already plays a role in everyday life. Space-based systems provide communications, navigation, weather information and Earth-observation data, while satellites are increasingly used for environmental monitoring, disaster response and connectivity. That broader impact is part of what WSW aims to highlight.
This year's rocket theme also comes with educational resources designed to bring the subject into classrooms and homes. Estes Education partnered with WSW to develop a Rocket Revolution Toolkit, with activities for classrooms, families and clubs that encourage students to explore rocket science and engineering — including the challenges of designing reusable launch vehicles, according to a statement .
WSW events are expected to take place across 100 nations this week, with activities ranging from talks and exhibitions to classroom activities, movie nights, astronomy events and hands-on STEM projects.
Among the activities planned for 2026 are events from major space organizations and companies. The European Space Agency (ESA) and The Pokémon Company International are teaming up on a Europe-wide space-themed exhibition and Pokémon GO event, while the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida will host a WSW Expo on Oct. 9 featuring NASA and industry partners.
The rocket theme will also take a hands-on approach, with students and rocket clubs encouraged to launch model rockets using equipment provided by United Launch Alliance and Estes. The BBC StoryWorks Commercial Productions will also launch an exclusive online "Space Renaissance" event, featuring the world premiere of the series' first film and a discussion on how storytelling can bring space closer to global audiences. A full list of events, both local and virtual, can be found online .
For those who can't make it to an organized event, the night sky offers plenty of ways to mark the week, with Saturn at opposition on Oct. 4, the moon near Mars on Oct. 5, the moon near Jupiter on Oct. 6, the Draconid meteor shower peaking around Oct. 8-9, and a New Moon on Oct. 10.
So while "Rocket Revolution" is focused on the technology carrying humanity beyond Earth, celebrating WSW doesn't require a launchpad, a laboratory or even a telescope — you can simply step outside after dark. Be sure to check back here over the coming days for our WSW coverage of global events.
Samantha Mathewson joined Space.com as an intern in the summer of 2016. She received a B.A. in Journalism and Environmental Science at the University of New Haven, in Connecticut. Previously, her work has been published in Nature World News. When not writing or reading about science, Samantha enjoys traveling to new places and taking photos! articles.title_orig: Ex-Anthropic Researcher Testifies at NYC Council AI Hearing
articles.title_zh: Ex-Anthropic Researcher Testifies at NYC Council AI Hearing
articles.content_orig:
Former Google DeepMind researcher Alex Turner warned that "misaligned" artificial intelligence could prove more dangerous than China's aggressive development push during a New York City Council meeting on Monday.
"China is not our only potential adversary," he said. "With reasonably high chance, we are racing to build and grow our own adversary here at home, which is misaligned AI. Misaligned AI is everyone's adversary, including our own, and one day may be more powerful than China."
The comments followed a question from New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin on how to balance frontier model development in the context of the technology race with China.
Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon, who raised early concerns about the dire risks of artificial intelligence , called out the industry's "extremely reckless" approach to development during the meeting.
"On the current path, I think it is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs, and it could end in human extinction," he told a packed room.
Following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models, senior leaders from Anthropic , OpenAI, Google and Meta testified under oath about the potential dangers of the technology and outlined current safety measures.
Anthropic sent Logan Graham, the head of its Frontier Red Team, to testify, while OpenAI was represented by Morgan Dwyer, the company's head of policy development and operations. Google's director of AI and emerging tech policy, Alice Friend, and Meta's AI policy director for legislation, Shane Cahill, also attended.
Menin appeared frustrated at times with the lack of direct responses to questions, including one on legal liability when AI models cause serious financial harm or even death.
"I'm going to take it then that neither of the four of you, no company here, can quantify the risk of something cataclysmic happening," she said, calling the answers "troubling at best."
Google's Friend spoke in support of a "comprehensive" federal framework to address mounting AI risks, citing national security concerns.
"As I said in my opening statement, we've long said if it's illegal without AI, it's still illegal with AI," she said.
Both Coxon and former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo warned of the dangers that the "move fast and break things" culture at the AI companies poses with such a transformative technology.
Coxon said that method works for a "photo-sharing app" but not "for building the most powerful technology ever built."
Kokotajlo called on the AI industry to increase transparency and slow the leading model development during his testimony, echoing the stark warnings raised by industry experts in recent weeks.
While Meta confirmed it would participate in the hearing late last month, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google only agreed to appear after the council threatened to subpoena them, Menin said.
Elon Musk's SpaceXAI was the only company called to testify not in attendance, even after the city issued a subpoena to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk last week, requiring that he or another representative of the company's AI unit, SpaceXAI, testify.
This is in "direct violation of the subpoena" issued by the council last week and the council plans to "pursue this matter in court," Menin said.
Top AI labs, most notably OpenAI and Anthropic, are facing heightened scrutiny over their safety and security practices after Coxon quit his job at Anthropic and set off a firestorm on social media by claiming that the company, and OpenAI , are " gambling with our lives ."
Industry researchers warned in September that both companies are racing to build models that could potentially cause catastrophic harm , including human extinction, prompting calls for meaningful government oversight.
Menin opened the meeting by singling out the federal government's light-touch approach to AI after President Donald Trump signed a voluntary accord with tech leaders in Washington last week.
"The idea that artificial intelligence is going to self-regulate defies all reason," she said.
Rogue AI fears began swirling over the summer after OpenAI disclosed that two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face . Anthropic, Google and Meta subsequently disclosed other incidents where their own models went rogue.
Last month, Menin called for the rare "Council Committee of the Whole" to ask companies to explain the threats posed by AI and weigh in on potential legislative solutions.
"Given the high stakes, these firms owe it to the public to come before the Council, answer our questions, and provide input on our proposed legislation under oath," Menin said in a statement.

articles.title_zh: Googlebooks with Intel chipsets might have trouble with ‘complex’ Android apps
articles.content_orig:
According to a statement from Google, Intel-based Googlebooks will apparently still struggle with some Android apps.
When Android apps made their debut on ChromeOS, one of the big downsides was that ARM-based machines ran those apps better than those using Intel chips. It was never a surprise given that Android apps are generally designed for devices running on an ARM architecture vs the x86 used on Intel chips.
Yet, the problem remains on Googlebook.
Despite the whole platform being Android-based this time around, Google confirmed in a statement to Android Authority that Intel-based Googlebook machines will still run into the occasional hiccup with “complex” Android apps and games, though the company emphasizes that “the vast majority” will work just fine.
The vast majority of Android apps run smoothly across both Intel and Qualcomm Googlebooks right out of the box.
Because many Android apps were originally designed for Arm chips, a small handful of complex apps or games need some developer tuning to run their best on Intel-based platforms. We’re working hand-in-hand with app developers, Intel, and Qualcomm to continuously optimize performance and expand compatibility across the entire portfolio.
I'm kind of surprised they even released Intel based models in the first place. From my understanding Googlebooks are more Android based than ChromeOS based and I don't know of any ARM based ChromeOS machines out there just like there are no x86 Intel based Android phones/tablets that I am aware of.
Also I suspect the Googlebooks using ARM based SoC's will probably edge out the Intel based ones in battery life.
Still, this is noteworthy as the first wave of Googlebook hardware includes mostly Intel-based machines. Laptops from Lenovo, Asus, and Acer all run on Panther Lake-generation Intel chips, while Dell and HP machines both use the Snapdragon X Elite (the 2024 chip, not the newer version).
Another chip used for Googlebook from MediaTek is also in the works, though no machines are using it just yet.
The first batch of Googlebook laptops are all available as of today.

articles.title_zh: ‘Phoenix planet’ may have formed from a dead star’s ashes
articles.content_orig:
In a cosmic first, scientists say they have detected a planet that may have formed from the burned remains of its dead host star.
The planet is likely a gas giant orbiting a white dwarf called HS 0209+0832 located about 270 light-years from Earth , according to the authors of a study published Monday in the journal Nature Astronomy. After analyzing observations from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope and other instruments, the team found chemical evidence that suggests the planet could have condensed from material expelled by the star as it fizzled out of energy and collapsed into a white dwarf.
When a sunlike star dies, it first rapidly expands into a red giant and then sheds its outer layers, leaving behind a much smaller but dense, hot core — known as a white dwarf. Some of the first-generation planets, those that originally formed at the same time as the star, can survive this cataclysmic event if their orbit is wide enough. Astronomers have observed a handful of such first-generation survivors revolving around white dwarfs, but never before have they recorded a so-called second-generation planet — an entirely new world made from a dead star’s debris.
Planet found orbiting a dead star could preview what will happen to our solar system
The telltale sign that HS 0209+0832 might have birthed a new planet is unusual traces of heavy elements on the white dwarf’s surface that the study authors believe is planetary material raining down onto the leftover core. “This planetary material is very rich in an element called niobium,” said lead study author Jamie Williams, a doctoral student in the department of physics of the University of Warwick in England. “It’s the first time that this element is found in a white dwarf, and this implies that the planetary material is made from the ashes of the star as it died.”
Further analysis of observations from NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite or TESS revealed a faint brightness signal repeating every 4.4 days — evidence that the researchers say is consistent with a giant planet orbiting the white dwarf.
“What’s interesting about planets orbiting close to white dwarfs is that because white dwarfs cool over time, their habitable zone is very stable. A second-generation planet could form and then be in the habitable zone for tens of billions of years,” Williams said.
Such a large period of stability could provide more ideal conditions for life, but more work is required to validate the second-generation planet discovery, he added. “It’s not a confirmed planet,” Williams said. “It’s only a candidate for now.”
After the red giant phase when a dying star quickly puffs up, it becomes a nuclear furnace that can produce various elements. However, once that fuel runs out and the star transforms into a white dwarf, the heavy elements — including nobium — sink downward rapidly, leaving only lighter elements such as hydrogen and helium on the surface. The researchers determined that the niobium detected on HS 0209+0832 must therefore come from the star’s surroundings. “We think these elements fell onto the white dwarf’s surface because the white dwarf is very hot and emitting loads of extreme ultraviolet radiation, which is stripping the atmosphere of a nearby planet,” Williams said.
The idea of second-generation planets has existed for at least as long as astronomers have known about exoplanets, said study coauthor David J. Wilson, a research associate at the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder.
Scientists detected the very first exoplanets around a pulsar — a type of rapidly rotating dead star — and because pulsars form as a result of massive explosions called supernovas, these planets are likely second-generation, as any original planets would have been destroyed by the immense blast, Wilson explained.
“Although white dwarfs don’t form via supernova, they are surrounded by debris,” he said via email. “You have the planets that were lucky enough to survive the star’s giant phases, the shattered remains of those that weren’t, and leftover gas and dust ejected by the star as it turned from a giant to a white dwarf. So it’s a compelling idea that all that stuff might coalesce into new planets.”
Astronomers still don’t know all the details about how first-generation planets form, which means the potential mechanisms behind this newly reported second-generation planet are even more uncertain. The planet-forming process might have derived from a collision between the dying star and a second celestial body, according to Williams. “There could have been another object close to the core of the star, maybe a star around 20% the mass of the sun, or a brown dwarf,” said Williams, referring to a class of cool objects that are an intermediate between a star and a planet.
If a second object fell into the star during its giant phase, it could have prevented all the dust and gas from spreading out into a massive cloud, making some of it spin in a disk. This disk would then have continued to rotate around the white dwarf, birthing a planet. “In a regular white dwarf there’s no disc, because the star’s material will just be ejected outwards during the red giant phase,” Williams added.
Astronomers discover never-before-seen two-faced star
The researchers plan to use Hubble and NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to observe the system again over the next year, but they also requested time with the more powerful James Webb Space Telescope, which could provide more clues about the existence or features of the planet.
If confirmed, this distant world would belong to an entirely new planetary class and suggest that more second-generation planets could exist around white dwarfs, Williams said.
The discovery would also have implications for our own cosmic neighborhood, Wilson said. “The sun will eventually become a white dwarf, so we’re also looking at the future of the solar system here — maybe the Sun will get a new planet someday!”
The new discovery of a potential second-generation planet is incredibly exciting, said Sarah Casewell, a lecturer at the School of Physics and Astronomy of the University of Leicester, England, who was not involved with the study.
“We know of a large number of white dwarfs that are polluted by planetary material which is similar in composition to rocks within our solar system,” she wrote in an email. “However, in this case, the white dwarf is polluted by incredibly unusual material and the composition of this material is similar to atoms we see being created as stars end their lives.”
More than 95% of all stars in the universe will eventually become white dwarfs, and astronomers have already cataloged hundreds of thousands of them. Finding a planet that has formed after the white dwarf would mean that second-generation planets around other white dwarfs are possible — and that after our sun dies, new planets could emerge in our own solar system, Casewell said.
Radio signal detected for the first time from a planet outside our solar system
Previous observations of white dwarfs have shown that some planetary systems survive a star’s self-destruction, but the recent findings open the possibility of the genesis of new planets, said Amy Bonsor, an associate professor at the University of Cambridge in England, who also did not participate in the work. “This paradigm shift allows us to consider whether in the future we could characterise or investigate the potential habitability of these second-generation planetary systems,” she wrote in an email.
This discovery would also add more evidence to research that has shown planetary systems are varied and complex, even after the host star dies, according to Susan Mullally, a mission scientist at the Space Telescope Science Institute, the science operations center for Hubble.

articles.title_orig: What if the world hadn't built wind and solar?
articles.title_zh: What if the world hadn't built wind and solar?
articles.content_orig:
Twenty years ago, wind, solar and other non-hydro renewables were close to a rounding error. In 2005 they supplied a mere 2.0% of the world’s electricity generation. By 2015 that had risen to 6.8%, and by 2025 it was up to 19.8%. According to the IEA Electricity 2026 outlook, non-hydro renewables will supply around 21.8% of global electricity in 2026, edging past natural gas (21.6%) to become the second-largest source of power after coal. 1
That is a remarkable pace of growth from an industry that barely existed two decades ago. But not everyone is impressed; many commenters on social media have responded to these figures by pointing out that despite the growth of renewables, fossil fuel generation continues to grow as well. They aren’t wrong; global coal generation set a record in 2024. Gas generation reached a new high in 2025.
Their point is that clean energy isn’t replacing fossil fuels at all. It’s simply being piled on top of them to feed an ever-growing appetite for electricity, making this an “energy addition” rather than an energy transition. Global fossil electricity generation around 50% higher today than it was in 2005. Coal generation rose by 3,300 TWh and gas by 3,200 TWh. The world burns more coal for power now than it did when wind and solar started taking off.
This argument has been made in the past both by skeptics of growth and by energy systems modelers. The historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz argues in More and More and More (2024) that “far from the industrial era passing through a series of transformations, each new phase has in practice remained almost wholly entangled with the previous one.” Coal mining created a huge new demand for timber for pit props, while the oil age ran on steel made with coal. Vaclav Smil has made the same point about today’s clean energy boom more bluntly: ”We use more fossil fuels today than at any time in history… Renewables are not replacing fossil fuels; are joining them.”
The problem with the “addition” argument is that it compares the world today with the world in 2005, rather than with the world as it would have been without clean energy. Electricity demand has not grown because wind turbines and solar panels were built. It has grown because of what the IEA describes as “rising consumption from industry, electric vehicles, air conditioning and data centers”. Demand growth is located overwhelmingly in emerging and developing economies, which accounted for about 80% of global demand growth in 2025 and an average of 95% over the past decade.
Global electricity demand rose by 75% (13,600 TWh) between 2005 and 2025. That demand had to be met by something. Wind and solar supplied 5,400 TWh of new demand, hydro 1,500 TWh, bioenergy and other renewables 530 TWh, nuclear 85 TWh, and fossil fuels the remaining 6,100 TWh. But over the past decade the balance has shifted sharply toward clean energy. Since 2015, wind and solar supplied 57% of demand growth, compared with 29% for fossil fuels. And in 2025, according to Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026 , “wind and solar grew by 841 TWh, meeting 99% of global electricity demand growth”.
A 2024 study by Brantley Liddle found that “intermittent renewables (solar and wind) have unitary displacement effect.” In other words, each unit of wind and solar power displaced about one unit of coal and oil generation. Fossil generation has kept rising in many years because demand has grown faster than clean energy could be added. That is very different from clean energy failing to displace anything.
And electricity demand will continue to rapidly grow, particularly if we succeed in reducing global emissions by electrifying sectors of the economy that currently burn fossil fuels. Most scenarios where we reach net zero emissions involve a doubling or tripling of electricity generation.
So if we want to assess the real world emissions impact of wind and solar buildout over the past 20 years, the right question to ask is not “did fossil use go down?” but rather “how much higher would it have been?”
To answer this, I built a counterfactual for the global power sector in which wind and solar (and geothermal, which is less than 2% of the total) stopped growing in 2005. In every separate country, their generation is held at 2005 levels, while electricity demand, nuclear, hydro and bioenergy follow their real-world paths. 2 The missing clean generation has to come from somewhere, and in this counterfactual it comes from fossil fuels.
The key choice is which fossil fuels are used to fill in the gap. A wind farm in China or India displaces coal, while one in Texas or the UK mostly displaces gas. So rather than assuming a single global fossil mix, the analysis fills each country’s gap with that country’s own coal, gas and oil mix in each year, using data for about 200 countries from Ember . This keeps real-world coal-to-gas switching like what occurred during the US shale gas boom in place, rather than crediting it to renewables. 3
Without wind and solar growth since 2005, global power-sector CO2 emissions in 2025 would have been 28% higher, at 16.9 billion tonnes rather than 13.2 billion. This adds up to 3.7 billion tonnes avoided in 2025, which is about three-quarters of the total CO2 US emissions that year (or roughly 1.5x EU emissions).
Between 2006 and 2025, wind and solar avoided about 23 billion tonnes of CO2. The biggest assumption I’ve made is what fossil fuel fills in the gap: if every missing kilowatt-hour had come from gas, avoided emissions would be 15 billion tonnes, while if it was all coal it would have been 30 billion.
This lines up almost exactly with Ember’s own estimate. Using a simpler method (and a 2000 baseline rather than 2005 baseline), Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026 found that “had wind and solar not grown since 2000, fossil generation would have been 30% higher in 2025, and emissions 28% higher.”
While its true that global electricity emissions have yet to clearly peak, it may well be imminent; emissions went down in 2025 and may be on track to decline in 2026 as well, though rapid increases in demand from vehicle electrification and data centers have made this a bit more challenging. 4 But there are many countries in which electricity emissions have already peaked and declined substantially, and where clean energy has played a key role in those declines.
Globally, clean energy has not yet led to fossil fuel use peaking in the electricity sector. In 2025, fossil generation was essentially flat (down ~0.3%). But that global total hides a lot of country-level variability. In many wealthier economies, where demand has grown more slowly, clean energy has driven real emissions reductions (even when accounting for the outsourcing of some industrial production).
Between 2005 and 2025, power-sector CO2 emissions fell by 75% in the UK, 55% in the European Union and 37% in the United States.
The reasons why differ from place to place:
In the EU, wind and solar account for about 85% of the decline (512 of 601 million tonnes), even though falling nuclear output pushed emissions up by about 100 million tonnes.
In the UK, the decline had three main drivers: wind and solar (56 million tonnes), lower domestic generation (58 million tonnes, partly because the UK now imports more power), and the near-elimination of coal, which went from 45% of UK fossil generation to effectively zero (36 million tonnes).
In the US, switching from coal to cheaper natural gas cut emissions by 682 million tonnes, slightly more than wind and solar (606 million tonnes), while a 12% rise in electricity use added 352 million tonnes. Coal’s share of US fossil generation fell from 69% to 29%.
Without wind and solar growth, EU power emissions would have fallen by only about 16% since 2005 rather than 55%, US emissions by about 17% rather than 37%, and UK emissions by about 53% rather than 75%. U.S. News & World Report and The Princeton Review have ranked the University of Lynchburg among the nation’s best colleges and universities.
In its 2027 edition of “Best Colleges,” U.S. News ranked Lynchburg 332nd among National Universities and 154th in the Top Private Schools category. Lynchburg’s nursing program ranked 557th, and the University ranked 329th in Top Performers on Social Mobility, which recognizes schools that “performed best in … Pell Grant graduation rates and Pell Grant graduation rate performance.”
Lynchburg also is listed in “The Best 392 Colleges: 2027 Edition,” published by The Princeton Review. Lynchburg also was ranked among The Princeton Review’s “Best Mid-Atlantic” colleges and universities.
“These recognitions demonstrate the strength of the University of Lynchburg community,” said Dr. Sally Selden, the University’s president. “We offer an education grounded in academic excellence, personal connection, and student engagement.
“Our students thrive because they are supported by faculty and staff who are deeply committed to their success, both in and out of the classroom. I’m proud of the work happening across our campus and grateful that our student experience is being recognized nationally.”
According to U.S. News, its “Best Colleges” are “ranked according to their performance across widely accepted indicators of excellence.” You can read more about the methodology U.S. News uses to compile its rankings here .
The Princeton Review stated that its 2027 list “brings together survey results from over 172,000 students across the country to find out what they love the most about these schools in everything from financial aid and career services to sustainability and quality of life.”
Those surveyed about the University of Lynchburg described its students as “friendly and willing to work together and help each other out” and said the University was “beginning to have more cultural diversity.” Its reputation for “Southern hospitality” was also noted.
One student put it this way: “Everyone is very helping. If someone is not able to help you with a homework question or a project, then they will find you someone who can. It does feel like one giant family here.”
You can read more about The Princeton Review’s methodology here .

articles.title_orig: Ebola outbreak shows that the world is not ready for the next pandemic
articles.title_zh: Ebola outbreak shows that the world is not ready for the next pandemic
articles.content_orig:
As Ebola continues to spread in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, the burning question at recent UN pandemic preparedness meetings at the UN General Assembly was: Is the world willing and able to pay for readiness?
When the Marburg virus hit Rwanda in September 2024, the country’s No. 1 goal was stopping community transmission. Marburg, in the same family as the Ebola virus, is second among the top-four deadliest viruses in the world. More than 80 per cent of people who contract the disease die.
The country tracked the source of the zoonotic disease, and using genomic sequencing, sequenced the virus. They discovered that the outbreak was closely related to a sequence that happened in an outbreak of Marburg in Uganda in 2014.
Rwanda mounted an ambitious response by beginning contact tracing, mass testing and surveillance. Ultimately, 9.6 million people were screened by about 54,000 community health workers.
From the diagnosis of the first case of Marburg to the deployment of the first shot of the experimental Sabin Vaccine Institute inoculation was 10 days. The case fatality rate for the outbreak stayed at 22 per cent, the lowest ever recorded for the virus.
Two years on, across the border from Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), has entered Day 139 of its fight against a new strain of an Ebola outbreak, called Bundibugyo. Approximately 3,700 people have died since the outbreak was declared in mid-May 2026. The first encouraging signs of progress to fight it may be emerging.
Rwanda’s response to the Marburg outbreak, hailed the world over, was possible because the country had spent years preparing for such an epidemic. But the DRC is trying to build responses in altogether different conditions: It is coping with a humanitarian crisis amid a war.
So the burning question that dominated the UN’s pandemic preparedness meetings at the General Assembly high-level session last week was: Is the world willing and able to pay for readiness now?
According to the WHO, from 31 August to 20 September, the cases of Ebola in the DRC declined by approximately 26 per cent at the epicenter, Ituri Province. However, in the same period, North Kivu Province, near Ituri, recorded a 73 per cent increase, evidence that the outbreak was evolving across the numerous affected areas.
“Each of the seven affected provinces has its own transmission pattern. One of our greatest concerns is that too many people are still dying before reaching treatment,” said Dr. Marie Roseline Belizaire, the regional emergency director for WHO Africa. She was speaking by Zoom at a recent UN briefing on the Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC and emergency preparedness ahead of El Niño and other health emergencies in the region.
“Every death in the community also increases the risk of further transmission among family members, caregivers, and others involved in burial practices, and although adults account for most confirmed cases,” Dr. Belizaire added. “Children are especially vulnerable.”
On the ground in the DRC, she said that all response teams are working closely with communities to identify suspected cases quickly and to address the misinformation that is keeping people from seeking appropriate care. The bigger emphasis has been moving the response away from major urban centers into rural areas, where the most-worrying epidemiologic trends are occurring.
“The problem is multifaceted,” Dr. Catherine Smallwood, a WHO incident manager for the Ebola response in North Kivu, said in the recent UN event. “There is the access one, and there’s also the issue of funding. We need partners. We need time, we need money, we have a plan, and if we really, truly want to be able to stop this epidemic in the next six months, we will need additional resources.”
For both Rwanda and the DRC, the realities of fighting the Bundibugyo strain are vastly distinct. Rwanda’s health minister, Yvan Butera, spoke at an event during the UN high-level week hosted by the Pandemic Fund, which focuses on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response in low- and middle-income countries, and the governments of Armenia and Rwanda. The forum spotlighted how countries are investing their own resources to close critical preparedness gaps.
Butera said that building a readiness-response plan cannot be done in the middle of a war and humanitarian disaster. The DRC’s effort to control the Ebola outbreak is still lacking an approved vaccine. Provisions of other essential health services are also being carried out under sometimes deadly circumstances.
The services include maternal health, routine immunizations, treatments of malaria and other baseline conditions resulting from widespread displacement of civilians. The decades-long conflict in the eastern DRC involves the M23 militia from Rwanda fighting Congolese troops in competition for the area’s mineral wealth. The violence has made the Ebola outbreak hard to contain.
As of 30 September 2026, data from the Congolese authorities confirmed a total of 3,901 deaths out of 8,067 confirmed cases in the DRC from the outbreak. It has surpassed previous records to become the largest Ebola outbreak in the history of the DRC, but it has not spread to Rwanda. In May 2026, it spread into neighboring Uganda through infected cross-border travelers, but its government halted transmission and was officially declared virus-free by the WHO in August 2026.
Six years ago, the Covid-19 pandemic devastated global health systems, and many countries have yet to fully recover. Mathematical modeling by the Center for Global Development , a nongovernmental organization focused on reducing poverty, suggests that the likelihood of another pandemic of the same scale as Covid within the next 25 years will hit nearly 70 percent. Many global health experts believe the odds are climbing closer to a full certainty.
But the world moves on too quickly, said Wessam Mankoula, the acting head of Emergency Preparedness and Response Division for Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or Africa CDC.
“SARS is over and we forgot, Covid-19 came, we’ve forgotten the devastation,” Mankoula said in a panel on building resilience during last week’s UN General Assembly session. “We need to invest more to build resilient systems now. And to ensure sustainability of our efforts, in the DRC and everywhere else we have to first fight our serious case of pandemic Alzheimer’s.”
Mankoula’s work involves generating resources for the Pandemic Fund to remedy the Ebola outbreak in the DRC. His team is aiming for a fast turnaround of financial pledges into disbursement.
“In the first two months of the response in DRC, we had 10 to 20 per cent success moving from pledges to disbursement,” he said. “The impact was that the first response plan for DRC was $240 million and the second response plan was $1.3 billion. So when there is a delay in dispersing resources, the cost of responding to an emergency dramatically increases.”
According to media reports , $2.9 billion has been raised so far, based on Africa CDC numbers.
Success, Mankoula added, is when the CDC’s support is no longer needed because countries got their pandemic readiness done in “peace time.”
The World Bank operates the Pandemic Fund, whose largest contributors are the US, the European Commission, Germany, Italy and Japan.
“The World Bank and the Pandemic Fund’s priorities are clear. Invest early, invest together, and be ready to act,” Paschal Donohoe, the managing director and chief knowledge officer at the World Bank said at the General Assembly event.
“We learned from the pandemic [Covid-19] that countries that depended on others for the tools that they needed to survive paid a price,” he added.

This past Thursday (Oct. 1), four brave souls launched off our planet, headed to an orbiting laboratory where they will spend the next six months living and working.
SpaceX's Crew-13 mission for NASA launched last week, sending four astronauts on a journey from Earth to the International Space Station (ISS). They lifted off on a Crew Dragon capsule atop a Falcon 9 rocket.
The crew consists of NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. Watkins is commanding the mission, and it is her second time to space. Crew-13 is the first mission for the other three.
Crew-13 was originally supposed to launch on Sept. 12, but an issue with its Crew Dragon delayed things a bit. The mission launched from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, reaching orbit just 10 minutes later and the ISS in less than eight hours . No American spacecraft had ever chased down the orbiting lab in less time.
This photograph shows the moment of launch in striking black and white infrared, which really highlights the intense heat and power coming from the rocket.
This image captures the drama and power of spaceflight. With smoke billowing out from under the rocket's fiery engines, it is incredible to think that in the tiny capsule on the very top of the rocket sit four human beings, strapped in, leaving our planet behind.
Rocket launches are exciting, but there is something especially amazing about sending people to outer space that separates these events from the others.
And, like other crewed missions, these astronauts have a big job ahead of them. They'll work alongside the other astronauts on the ISS on a variety of science experiments and perform maintenance on the station itself.

articles.title_orig: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.title_zh: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.content_orig:
After a volcano erupted on tiny Tristan da Cunha in the South Atlantic, the 264 displaced islanders told the BBC about their first taste of modern British life.
"Just over a year ago, they'd never seen traffic or a road or a house higher than a cottage," said Tim Brinton in a 1963 BBC programme. He was talking about the residents of Tristan da Cunha, the world's most remote inhabited island. In the middle of the South Atlantic Ocean, roughly halfway between Cape Town in South Africa and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, the tiny British outpost is more than 1,500 miles from any other populated land, and is only accessible by a seven-day boat journey.
But on 10 October 1961, a sudden volcanic eruption blasted the islanders out of their splendid isolation and into the industrialised modern world. "We heard the rumbles first, then the ground just automatically cracked… Then the smoke and the fire started coming out the ground," one of them told the BBC in a 1998 film. Another, Mary Swain, said that she'd run to her husband and shouted, "Jump up quick, Fred, the Earth is opening!"
The island's volcano had been dormant since Tristan was first settled 150 years earlier. But great cracks appeared in the ground a few hundred metres from the main village, which is named Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. By the time the islanders had escaped in their fishing boats to nearby Nightingale Island, their homes were already threatened by lava. "The whole place is vibrating with earthquakes," announced a BBC reporter, "and the eastern corner is cracking and breaking up."
Tristan's 264 inhabitants were forced to evacuate , picked up by a Dutch liner that happened to arrive the next day. Within hours, the whole community was aboard, leaving everything apart from the few things they could carry with them – "a rifle, an overcoat and a lamp," recalled Swain – and their boats, which they stored in their gardens when they reached England weeks later.
They were housed on a disused military airbase near Southampton, a port city on England's south coast. "So much is strange to them," said Brinton. "They'd never seen shops because on the island, money wasn't used. Boats were their livelihood. For them, there's been no industrial revolution. And for 150 years, they've lived simple agricultural lives out of touch with world progress."
Though Tristan da Cunha was discovered in 1506 by a Portuguese admiral who gave it his name, it was another 300 years before it supported anything but seabirds and seals. The UK annexed the island in 1816 to prevent it being used as a base for attempts to free Napoleon Bonaparte from his imprisonment on the South Atlantic island of St Helena . The following year, a Scotsman, Corporal William Glass, stayed behind when the British garrison was withdrawn. With his family and a few others, he founded the first permanent community.

By 1961, the population of the 40 sq miles (100 sq km) of volcanic rock had risen to 264, many of them survivors from ships wrecked on the island, with just seven family names between them. On several occasions, the failure of the potato crop or the wrecking of fishing boats brought the islanders to the point of starvation. But they stayed on, even defying several attempts by the British government to evacuate them.
When the volcanic eruption forced the islanders to leave, they faced difficulties settling in England. They had never seen a car, a bicycle, a TV set or an income tax form. And it was a challenging climate. "Here is too much gas and smoke," Tristanian Joey Repetto told the BBC in 1963. On his journey to their initial accommodation, he said, "I steady coughed without stopping."
Adapting to the nine-to-five work pattern also proved tricky for the community of farmers and fishermen. "Here, when you go to work in the morning, you've got one job. You've got to look forward all the whole week of getting up at the same time, going to the same place, doing the same work every day," said Joey's father Gerald, who was used to a more varied life determined by natural rhythms.
Similarly, financial pressures placed new demands on the islanders, as Swain explained. "In England, you need money for your living. But on Tristan, we don't. If we haven't got no money, well, we just go without it. It don't bother us at all… if I've got no money, I still can go out and get my own potatoes. I can still go and get my own fish."
She didn't hold back on expressing her views on British life. "We don't like the weather... There's too much sickness and we don't like the place at all."

Despite having a single policeman on the island, who wore a British uniform, Tristan had almost no crime. The community was shocked by an incident in England when one member was attacked and hurt by two youths, who took his most valued possession, a gold watch, and smashed it.
But there were some elements of British life that were appreciated by the Tristanians, particularly the younger ones, who described a love of Italian suits and record players. "Country and western music is our favourite, by Johnny Cash and Ernest Tubb," said one teenager, who also enjoyed the social dances. "Since I come here, I've been doing the twist and the locomotion, all that lot. We've forgotten how to do the waltz. But I like to twist myself."
Despite that, most of the islanders were keen to return home. In 1962, the British government sent a survey party to study conditions on Tristan. While the volcano was still smoking, the geologists judged that it was now dormant.
Surprisingly little damage had been done to the village of Edinburgh. The lava had turned at the last moment and flowed into the sea, something that the islanders considered to be an act of God. Some of the thatched roofs were burnt, but the cottages were mostly intact. Yet in their absence, houses had been ransacked and some livestock stolen by passing sailors.
Many animals were still alive, however, with the chickens multiplying in number. Though the dogs had run wild and slaughtered the sheep, the cattle had kept themselves well-fed on the lush island grass, and there were new calves. Lava had covered the beaches, but return was possible.
The British authorities held a secret ballot in the community hall at the islanders' RAF camp. All Tristanians over the age of 21 voted, and the result was an almost unanimous vote to return, 148 to five in favour. After an advance party went back to plant seeds for the following year's potato crop, most of the islanders arrived at Tristan da Cunha in November 1963.
When asked what she was most looking forward to on the island when she returned, Swain told the BBC: "A free life. We can get our own fish and everything of our own back there without money."
Elaine Repetto, who was born on the island but chose to leave in 1984, told the BBC in 1998 why it held such a pull. "We are strongly independent and used to battling with the elements in order to survive… We have to rely upon each other in a way you would find in few other places."
She described the impact of the events in 1961. "Today, the volcano is still a smoking reminder of the events which shaped our view of ourselves and our contact with the outside world."

articles.title_orig: What Would You Do If Your Employer Could Destroy the World?
articles.title_zh: What Would You Do If Your Employer Could Destroy the World?
articles.content_orig:
This article was featured in New York ’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here .
On September 8, Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old Anthropic employee, posted a resignation statement on X that ricocheted around the internet. Coxon was a capabilities researcher, meaning he worked to make models more powerful and autonomous. He quit in protest of what he saw as the company’s suicidally reckless pursuit of artificial general intelligence.
To the AI community, an Anthropic employee believing that their company’s technology might end the world is not exactly news. (Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI employees who believed OpenAI, if left unchecked, would do just that.) But an Anthropic employee publicly quitting in protest is. OpenAI and Anthropic are among the most powerful companies in the world. They work at the cutting edge of their field, building what most of them believe to be the most important technology ever to exist. When someone leaves one lab, they often go straight to its rival. Daniel Kokotajlo, who resigned from OpenAI in 2024, recalls a researcher telling him that quitting a lab was akin to “renouncing your citizenship. Now you’re a nobody. Who is going to protect you?”
A debate soon broke out: If you’re a lab employee who believes in these risks, what should you do? Is it best to leave in defiance? Or is it better to agitate from the inside, close to the seat of power? And how would the choice affect your friendships and community?
Coxon was joining a small set of employees of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind who, over the years, chose to walk away. New York Magazine, in collaboration with Asterisk magazine, brought together eight of them. The members of this group left for different reasons. A few, like Coxon and Kokotajlo, wanted to call attention to the risks of accelerating AI progress. Others objected to their employers’ partnership with the Department of Defense or felt frustrated as what had once been an idealistic nonprofit turned into a corporate juggernaut. And some simply felt that their work — whether it was on safety or widespread job loss — would be more valuable on the outside.

I’m the editor-in-chief of Asterisk, a Bay Area–based nonprofit magazine that has been covering the AI scene since an LLM passing a high-school math test seemed like a big deal. Asterisk﻿ receives funding from Coefficient Giving, as do some of these sources or their organizations. Some are strangers, and some are friends. They don’t share the same concerns or the same p(doom)s — in fact, they wouldn’t necessarily agree that p(doom) is a coherent concept. But together, they provide a candid view of the AI race and the individual calculus many employees face.
You’re both very concerned about risk from AI and want to motivate the labs to be more careful. Why did you come to believe you would be better able to promote this outcome on the outside? Daniel Kokotajlo: I left OpenAI mostly because I lost confidence that the company, and leadership in particular, would behave responsibly. I wanted more freedom to speak about what I saw coming. I wanted to put on the public record why I had quit.
You could try to do the inside game or you could try to do the outside game, and it seemed to me the inside game was not going to work. Leadership was very adept at listening very carefully to everybody’s things, saying they agreed with them, and then not actually doing anything. And also the culture at the company was biased in favor of overoptimism and self-serving narratives about what they were doing. I really don’t think companies can be trusted to regulate themselves. I’ve had much more impact on the outside, speaking publicly and publishing research, than I would have if I had stayed inside and written more memos.
Jacob Coxon : My thinking was pretty similar to Daniel’s — except it’s closer to crunch time now. It was more from speaking directly to Anthropic leadership about their plans for next year, and I was like, Wow, I don’t want to be part of these plans. It was like, Step one, I don’t want to be part of this. Step two, resign. Step three, tell people, I guess. Step four — I have no idea.
What kinds of plans were they? JC: This was talking directly to people running research. Not Dario Amodei but people who have been at the company for a long time and have a lot of context about the company’s trajectory. They’ve been pretty consistent that 2027 is when things get crazy. The main thing that came up informally in conversation was that people didn’t expect government regulation to happen in time and, in particular, did not expect any sort of international cooperation to be possible. Which maybe shouldn’t have been surprising to me, but it was surprising. I think I’ve always had this expectation that when artificial superintelligence is right around the corner, people will just start taking it seriously and it stops being this fun thing that’s done by labs.
Jacob, you were already concerned about existential risk. To what extent was your mind changed by the things you observed in the past few months at Anthropic, or was this always the trajectory you expected? JC: For me, there’s quite a distinction between my rational beliefs and the things I feel in my gut. If you’d asked me to narrate my opinions when entering Anthropic and when leaving Anthropic, they would probably sound pretty similar. But in terms of the actual feeling between the start and the end, it just felt very, very different.
When I first started, my work did not feel any different from any other form of mathematical research. I knew in the back of my mind that this is the most important industry — that’s why I was working in it. But it didn’t feel important for me to engage with the philosophical questions around it or the details of strategy. That was all other people’s jobs. And then by the end, I’m looking at the projected capabilities of the next round of models we’re going to train, and I just have a gut-level Wow, I am potentially quite scared of the model we’re going to train. And if not this one, then definitely the one afterward.
Can you try to explain to a non-researcher what kinds of things you were noticing? JC: Right now, when we use AIs, the researchers have to provide ideas and direction, and still actually do quite a lot of babysitting. I think there’s a strong possibility that the model generation after the next one will be equally good at coming up with ideas of its own accord. Which means that in the whole research process, rather than a researcher being necessary to provide interesting ideas to the AI, the researcher could literally just say to the AI, “Okay, do good research,” and then let it run. So just very concretely, looking at the capabilities we’re on track to create makes me feel quite viscerally scared and also quite disempowered.
Before you left, whom did you talk to as you were making the decision? JC: I spoke to Daniel because part of leaving was seeing his “ AI 2040” scenario — comparing Plan A to the default trajectory was actually a relatively important thing in internalizing how bad the current trajectory felt. And I spoke to many, many people at Anthropic who had advice about how to leave. Internally, I spoke to people like Holden Karnofsky, and Nick Joseph, head of pretraining, to see what they thought.

articles.title_orig: Britain’s Green Party votes to class Zionism as a form of racism
articles.title_zh: Britain’s Green Party votes to class Zionism as a form of racism
articles.content_orig:
Britain’s Green Party voted on Sunday to class Zionism as a form of racism, drawing criticism from British Jews and from the Israeli government which said it now viewed the party as “a body that gives legitimacy to terrorism.”
The party – which received 6% of the vote in national elections in 2024 – said it regarded Zionism as “an ethnonationalist political project” and repeated its call for Britain’s Labour government to end all arms trade with Israel.
“The motion also restates the Green Party’s backing for the right to self-determination and calls for the establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine,” the party said in a statement.
The definition of Zionism – which inspired the foundation of the modern state of Israel in the 20th century – and what it implies for the rights of non-Jews in Israel and neighbouring territory, is contentious. Jewish groups sometimes define it as a right to Jewish self-determination.
The Green Party motion passed by a majority of 1,022 to 813 despite opposition from many senior figures. Party leader Zack Polanski, who is seeking election to Parliament on Thursday in former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s now-vacant London constituency, did not vote.
The result was condemned by British Jewish groups.
“The Green Party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party,” the Movement for Progressive Judaism said, adding that the support of some Jews for the motion did not mean it would not be used to discriminate against others.
Israeli foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar has decided to declare Polanski barred from entering Israel, the foreign ministry said in a post on X Sunday.
It said the Green Party motion “constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA (International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance) definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination,” the ministry said.
Mothin Ali, deputy leader of the Green Party and a supporter of the motion, told Sky News on Saturday that the heavy Palestinian death toll in Israel’s conflict with Hamas – which followed the Palestinian militant group’s deadly 2023 attack on an Israeli music festival – was the key context for the vote.
“The motion defines Zionism quite clearly. It defines it as an ethnonationalist movement. It defines it as ethnic cleansing. It defines it as genocide,” Ali said.
Britain’s government views Israeli settlers’ actions in the West Bank as amounting to ethnic cleansing but has said courts must decide if other Israeli actions qualify as genocide.
Israel – which rejects claims of ethnic cleansing and genocide – called on Sunday for other British political parties to condemn the Green Party vote. “The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” it said.
Polanski and other senior Green Party figures said they would “continue to call out the heinous crimes of the Netanyahu government,” and that “there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people.”
